study_design.design_type_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled 2-period crossover trial; 6-week treatment periods separated by 6-week washout

arms.label: Fludrocortisone acetate
arms.dose: 0.1 mg initially; doubled to 0.2 mg after 2 weeks if no improvement

arms.label: Placebo
arms.dose: Matched placebo; capsule number doubled after 2 weeks if no improvement

study_design.randomization_method: A simple random assignment table was derived by means of SPSS 6.01 for Windows.

source_design_and_timing.report: A Preliminary Placebo-Controlled Crossover Trial of Fludrocortisone for Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
source_design_and_timing.design: Random-allocation, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial.
source_design_and_timing.treatment_sequence: Participants were randomly assigned initially to fludrocortisone or placebo for 6 weeks, followed by a 6-week washout, then the opposite treatment for 6 weeks.
source_design_and_timing.randomization: Simple random assignment table generated with SPSS 6.01 for Windows; randomization completed in the Drug Evaluation Unit by an individual other than the project research assistant.
source_design_and_timing.blinding: Patients, clinical research staff, investigators, and treatment-preparing pharmacists were blinded; code remained unbroken until study termination. Data analysts knew assignment groups needed for comparison but not which was active.
source_design_and_timing.eligibility: CFS diagnosis based on case-definition criteria. Excluded if fatigue severity during preceding month was less than 5 on a 0-10 scale or if taking fludrocortisone, antihypertensives, antidepressants, anxiolytics, or corticosteroids.
source_design_and_timing.assessment_timing: Symptoms, SF-36, PANAS, reaction time, and treadmill testing assessed at beginning and end of each 6-week arm. Blood pressure, heart rate, and norepinephrine measured at baseline; blood pressure and heart rate also recorded at treadmill termination and subsequent visits.
source_design_and_timing.exercise_protocol: Treadmill at 1 mph, maximum 30 minutes, stopping earlier for exhaustion.
source_design_and_timing.baseline_posture_protocol: Supine after 15 minutes rest; standing after 5 minutes upright; postexercise at treadmill termination.
source_design_and_timing.recruitment_timing: Registries established July 1988 and 1989; recruitment questionnaires mailed January-February 1996.

source_dose_and_delivery.active_treatment: Fludrocortisone acetate, scheduled 0.1-0.2 mg per treatment arm.
source_dose_and_delivery.escalation: If no fatigue improvement after 2 weeks, dose of drug or placebo doubled.
source_dose_and_delivery.formulation: Florinef (Apothecon), 0.1-mg tablet placed in size 1 light-blue opaque gelatin capsule and filled with lactose.
source_dose_and_delivery.administration: Oral capsules; patients instructed not to open them.
source_dose_and_delivery.diet: Participants instructed not to change diet, including salt intake.
source_dose_and_delivery.cointerventions: No additional salt intervention or other treatment modalities were included.

key_inclusion_criteria: Chronic fatigue syndrome diagnosis according to published case-definition criteria
Fatigue severity during preceding month of at least 5 on a 10-cm visual analogue scale
key_exclusion_criteria: Use of antihypertensives, antidepressants, anxiolytics, or corticosteroids

per_arm.analysis_population: 20 paired participants completing both treatment periods; not independent arms
20 paired participants completing both treatment periods; not independent arms

analysis_population.efficacy_exclusions: All 5 withdrawals were excluded from treatment-efficacy evaluation.

source_flow_figure.description: Flow through randomized placebo-controlled crossover trial. Registered patients n=261; responded n=120; declined participation n=43; eligible patients n=30; not randomized n=5, with reasons n=1 as printed; randomization shown as R. Placebo allocation: received as allocated n=24, did not receive as allocated n=1, withdrawn for ovarian surgery n=1, withdrawn during washout for family problems n=1, completed arm n=24, completed both arms n=20. Fludrocortisone allocation: received as allocated n=22, did not receive as allocated n=3, withdrawn for worsening symptoms n=3, withdrawn during washout n=0, completed arm n=22, completed both arms n=20.
source_flow_figure.plot_only_coordinates: Not applicable; diagram counts are available.

source_table3.caption: Baseline Blood Pressure, Heart Rate, and Norepinephrine Levels
footnotes: Values obtained at baseline in 25 participants with CFS between 9 and 11 AM: supine after 15 minutes rest, standing after 5 minutes upright, then treadmill at 1 mph to exhaustion or 30 minutes.

source_baseline.mean_age_summary: Mean age approximately 40 years in abstract; 39.7 ± 10.9 years in Results.
source_baseline.illness_duration: 7.0 years in abstract; 7.0 ± 4.9 years in Results.
source_baseline.comparison_registry: No significant differences in age, sex, illness duration, or functional impairment versus 190 nonparticipating CFS patients in the Minnesota Regional CFS Research Program registry.
source_baseline.baseline_function: Marked functional impairment; most symptom ratings greater than 5; distance before exhaustion approximately 2 to 3 blocks on average.
source_baseline.baseline_biomarker: Supine norepinephrine 1632 ± 608 nmol/L; standing 2780 ± 953 nmol/L; postexercise 2936 ± 1050 nmol/L in Table 3, versus 2933 ± 1050 nmol/L in narrative.

complete_source_table3.caption: Baseline Blood Pressure, Heart Rate, and Norepinephrine Levels
footnotes: Values obtained at baseline in 25 participants with CFS between 9 and 11 AM: supine after 15 minutes rest, standing after 5 minutes upright, then treadmill at 1 mph to exhaustion or 30 minutes.

source_narrative.finding: Baseline plasma norepinephrine increased from 1632 ± 608 nmol/L supine to 2780 ± 953 standing and 2933 ± 1050 nmol/L after exercise in narrative text. reported_results.note: Baseline postural physiology and external controls are not randomized treatment arms. Postexercise NE differs: Table 2936±1050 versus narrative2933±1050.

title: A Preliminary Placebo-Controlled Crossover Trial of Fludrocortisone for Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
authors: Peterson PK; Pheley A.; Schroeppel J.; Schenck C.; Marshall P.; Kind A.; Haugland JM; Lambrecht LJ; Swan S.; Goldsmith S.

release_limitations.reason: Source data have been reviewed. Documented source limitations and synthesis decisions still prevent numerical conclusions.

study_design.design_type_detail: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled 2-period crossover trial with subsequent open-label phase
study_design.randomization_method: Randomized crossover; procedure not described
study_design.setting: single-center outpatient study at University of California Irvine Medical Center

source_design_and_timing.condition: Chronic fatigue syndrome defined using proposed CDC criteria.
source_design_and_timing.design: Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, two-period crossover.
source_design_and_timing.sequence: Each participant received one preparation for 1 week, then the alternate preparation for the next week; the allocation sequence is not reported.
periods: Week 1: 1-week supply of prefilled syringes containing either LEFAC or placebo.
After week 1: syringe count and second questionnaire.
After week 2: syringe return and third questionnaire.
Elective open-label extension: offered daily LEFAC for 2 weeks and fourth questionnaire.
source_design_and_timing.blinding: LEFAC and placebo were identical in appearance; administration was double blind during the randomized phase.
source_design_and_timing.carryover: No carryover assessment or sequence-specific analysis is reported.

source_dose_and_delivery.active_treatment: Bovine liver extract, 10 µg/mL cyanocobalamin equivalent, with folic acid 0.4 mg/mL and cyanocobalamin 100 µg/mL.
source_dose_and_delivery.frequency: Daily during the reported open-label extension; each blinded period supplied 1 week of syringes.
source_dose_and_delivery.duration: 1 week LEFAC and 1 week placebo in crossover sequence, followed by optional 2 weeks of open-label daily LEFAC.
source_dose_and_delivery.placebo: Identical in appearance; composition not reported.
source_dose_and_delivery.combination_context: The authors state that community use often combined LEFAC with dietary manipulation, stress reduction, and other medications; this study did not evaluate those combinations.

key_inclusion_criteria: Adults meeting proposed Centers for Disease Control criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome
Fatigue reducing daily activity to less than 50% of premorbid levels for at least 6 months
No medical or psychiatric condition or medication accounting for fatigue or symptom complex
At least six specified accompanying symptoms
Normal laboratory evaluation including blood counts, chemistry, sedimentation rate, thyrotropin, rheumatoid factor, and urinalysis
key_exclusion_criteria: Medical or psychiatric condition or medication accounting for fatigue or symptom complex

per_arm.analysis_population: 14 paired participants; randomized sequence sizes unreported
14 paired participants; randomized sequence sizes unreported

source_participant_flow.dropout_detail: Completed the blinded phase but did not return the third questionnaire and was excluded from analysis.
source_participant_flow.enrollment_stopped: Enrollment stopped at 15 subjects to permit data analysis before recruiting additional participants.

source_narrative.text: In an unpublished 1987 preliminary open-label study of 9 patients with CFS, all 9 reportedly had dramatic symptom alleviation within a few days when up to 2 mL of LEFAC was injected intramuscularly daily. In the discussion, the authors state that all 9 improved within 1 week at the dose used in the blinded study.

reported_results.note: Separate 1987 pilot; not part of the 15-person randomized trial and not an independent randomized comparison.

outcomes.synthesis_population: Adults meeting Centers for Disease Control criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome

source_narrative.text: Using paired t tests and assuming a 10% difference in scoring on any scale was clinically significant, the likelihood of a type II error was P<.15. Assuming a 20% difference was clinically significant, the likelihood was P<.025. The authors state that 10% and 20% corresponded to 50% and 100% of the estimated SD, respectively.

reported_results.note: Author type-II error claims, not observed efficacy P values. Enrollment stopped for analysis before recruiting further participants.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: The randomization procedure was not described and one participant was excluded from analysis after failing to return the third questionnaire.

source_narrative.injection_reactions: The authors state that none of the subjects experienced adverse reactions to injections.

subject_12.event: Temperature of 38.9°C after 2 days of open-label LEFAC.
subject_12.preceding_treatment: Had received placebo during week 2 immediately before open-label LEFAC.
subject_12.outcome: Recovered uneventfully within a few days.

source_narrative.denominators: No separate safety-analysis denominator, event table, laboratory safety results, or systematic adverse-event ascertainment details are reported.

open_label_events.causal_attribution: Not classified by authors as an injection reaction

summary: This 15-person crossover trial analyzed 14 paired questionnaire responders and found no significant LEFAC–placebo difference on four outcomes. Eleven completed an elective open-label extension. All 16 reported P values and 14 baseline rows are retained; source-image review corrected a symptom P value and baseline transcription errors. No treatment means or effect-size uncertainty were reported.

Removed duplicated 15/15 randomized-arm counts and kept the shared paired population.
Separated open-label fever from randomized harms and corrected ongoing open-label treatment timing.
Retained all paired P values, separate pilot response and author power claims.

completion.limitations: All supplied pages, tables, figure annotations and own-study numerical narrative reviewed. Exact graph-only coordinates remain unavailable; source inconsistencies and missing analysis denominators remain explicit. No declared missing supplement identified.

release_limitations.reason: Source data have been reviewed. Documented source limitations and synthesis decisions still prevent numerical conclusions.

arms.label: Hydrocortisone
arms.dose: 13 mg/m2 every morning and 3 mg/m2 every afternoon

study_design.randomization_method: Randomization was done in blocks of 10 subjects.

source_design_and_timing.report: Low-Dose Hydrocortisone for Treatment of Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: A Randomized Controlled Trial
source_design_and_timing.design: Randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind therapeutic trial
source_design_and_timing.setting: Single-center tertiary-care research institution; NIH Warren Grant Magnuson Clinical Center
source_design_and_timing.study_period: Conducted between 1992 and 1996; treatment began between May 1992 and December 1995.
eligibility: Age 18-55 years.
1988 CDC CFS case criteria; authors state all would also meet the more liberal 1994 criteria.
Illness onset over 6 weeks or less.
No contraindications to systemic steroids.
No other acute or chronic medical or psychiatric condition requiring ongoing or intermittent medication.
Most over-the-counter and prescription medications, except acetaminophen, proscribed for 2-6 weeks before enrollment and throughout the study.
Effective birth control and negative pregnancy test required for women.
Active depression severe enough to warrant treatment excluded enrollment.
source_design_and_timing.blinding: Double blind; study code was not broken when tapering treatment was initiated.
source_design_and_timing.visits: Patients were admitted twice: for eligibility confirmation and treatment initiation, and at treatment completion.
source_design_and_timing.treatment_duration: Approximately 12 weeks; weekly adverse-event records for 12 weeks; remaining treated patients received 76-96 days.
source_design_and_timing.open_label_extension: Patients with posttreatment stimulated cortisol <276 nmol/L (<10 µg/dL) received a 6-week tapering regimen of open-label hydrocortisone, followed by repeat stimulation testing. This was safety rescue/follow-up, not a randomized extension.
outcomes: Primary efficacy centered on Wellness score improvement by any amount and by 5, 10, and 15 points, plus change in mean score during treatment.
Secondary outcomes: other self-rating scales, adverse symptoms, basal cortisol, and cosyntropin-stimulated cortisol.

source_dose_and_delivery.reported_body_surface_area_dose: 13 mg/m² every morning and 3 mg/m² every afternoon.
source_dose_and_delivery.reported_fixed_approximate_schedule: About 16 mg/m²/day; 20-30 mg every morning at about 8 AM and 5 mg every day at about 2 PM, for 12 weeks.
source_dose_and_delivery.comparator: Placebo pills on the same schedule.
source_dose_and_delivery.intended_physiology: Approximate normal daily cortisol levels and diurnal variation; estimated about 30% net daily increase in CFS patient cortisol exposure.
source_dose_and_delivery.dose_as_discussed_in_comment: 25-35 mg/day, equivalent to approximately 6 mg prednisone.
source_dose_and_delivery.monitoring: Daily/weekly self-rating and adverse-event forms; basal morning cortisol and serum cortisol 1 hour after cosyntropin before treatment and at treatment end.
source_dose_and_delivery.rescue_delivery: Patients were instructed to request stress doses during emergencies and were given Medic Alert bracelets. Patients below the stimulated cortisol threshold received a 6-week open-label taper.

key_inclusion_criteria: Age 18 to 55 years
Met 1988 CDC criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome
Illness began over a period of 6 weeks or less
No contraindications to systemic steroids
key_exclusion_criteria: Other acute or chronic medical or psychiatric condition requiring medication
Use of most over-the-counter and prescription drugs
Peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, hypertension, glaucoma, diabetes, or untreated tuberculosis

source_flow_figure.printed_text: A total of 638 subjects were screened and 70 were enrolled, with 35 placed in each treatment arm. Seven patients withdrew from the study, leaving 63 to comply with their assigned treatments.

results: Improvement in mean Wellness score: placebo 19/35 (54.3%) versus hydrocortisone 20/30 (66.7%), P = .31.
Wellness improvement thresholds: at least 5 points, hydrocortisone 53% versus placebo 29%, P = .04; at least 10 points, 33% versus 14%, P = .07; at least 15 points, 20% versus 6%, P = .08.
Mean Wellness improvement: hydrocortisone 6.3 points versus placebo 1.7 points, P = .06.
The daily average Wellness improvement was greater for hydrocortisone than placebo on every treatment day across 12 weeks; comparison of numbers of days favored hydrocortisone, P < .001 by Sign test.
No statistically significant treatment differences were found for other self-rating scales or subscales.

between_group_effects.effect_quote: showed suboptimal responses to cosyntropin challenge at the end of treatment (P,.001 by 2-sided Fisher exact test).

results: Baseline basal and cosyntropin-stimulated cortisol levels were well matched between groups.
Placebo recipients showed no obvious changes in basal or stimulated cortisol during treatment.
Completion basal morning serum cortisol: placebo 408 (152) nmol/L [14.8 (5.5) µg/dL] versus hydrocortisone 279 (179) nmol/L [10.1 (6.5) µg/dL], P = .002.
Completion cortisol response to cosyntropin: placebo 869 (102) nmol/L [31.5 (3.7) µg/dL] versus hydrocortisone 577 (248) nmol/L [20.9 (9.0) µg/dL], P < .001.
Five patients had posttreatment stimulated cortisol <276 nmol/L (<10 µg/dL); all had been randomized to hydrocortisone and began a 6-week open-label taper.
Seven additional patients had posttreatment stimulated cortisol 276-497 nmol/L (10-18 µg/dL); all had received hydrocortisone.

reported_results.note: These are adrenal-response findings, not counts of serious clinical events. No recovery result after the taper is supplied.

outcomes.name: Daily pattern of Wellness improvement
outcomes.synthesis_population: Adults meeting 1988 CDC chronic fatigue syndrome criteria

source_figure2.description: Daily plot over 12 treatment weeks of the difference between hydrocortisone and placebo means in change of Wellness score from the pretreatment mean. The printed interpretation states that hydrocortisone Wellness scores increased more than placebo scores on every treatment day.
source_figure2.printed_result: Hydrocortisone recipients improved quickly and sustained a greater increase in Wellness scores than placebo recipients for every day of the 12 treatment weeks.
source_figure2.plot_only_coordinates: Exact daily coordinates unavailable without guessing.

results: Improvement in mean Wellness score: placebo 19/35 (54.3%) versus hydrocortisone 20/30 (66.7%), P = .31.
Wellness improvement thresholds: at least 5 points, hydrocortisone 53% versus placebo 29%, P = .04; at least 10 points, 33% versus 14%, P = .07; at least 15 points, 20% versus 6%, P = .08.
Mean Wellness improvement: hydrocortisone 6.3 points versus placebo 1.7 points, P = .06.
The daily average Wellness improvement was greater for hydrocortisone than placebo on every treatment day across 12 weeks; comparison of numbers of days favored hydrocortisone, P < .001 by Sign test.
No statistically significant treatment differences were found for other self-rating scales or subscales.

reported_results.note: Daily group means rather than independent participant responders; exact plotted coordinates unavailable.

model_tests.test: Sign test comparing days on which average improvement favored each group

outcomes.name: Associations of Wellness change with other score changes
outcomes.outcome_concept: Associations of Wellness change with other score changes
outcomes.synthesis_population: Adults meeting 1988 CDC chronic fatigue syndrome criteria

results: Changes in Wellness score correlated with Profile of Mood States Fatigue, r = −0.56, P < .001; Confusion, r = −0.42, P < .001; Beck Depression Inventory, r = −0.42, P < .001; Sickness Impact Profile, r = −0.45, P < .001; Activity scale, r = 0.37, P = .003; and Profile of Mood States Vigor, r = 0.53, P < .001.
Correlations were generally similar for all treated subjects combined and for hydrocortisone or placebo separately; detailed subgroup values were not provided.

Baseline serum cortisol and baseline stimulated cortisol responses were not associated with clinical severity or response. For hydrocortisone recipients, correlations of Wellness change with both baseline serum cortisol levels were r = 0.05, P = .81, and with baseline stimulated cortisol response r = 0.05, P = .79.
The lowest cortisol levels and adrenal reserve were not associated with greater symptoms or greater likelihood of response.

reported_results.note: Spearman associations, not treatment contrasts; separate arm coefficients are described but not printed.

source_table3.caption: Adverse Reactions to Hydrocortisone or Placebo Treatment

source_narrative.clinical_adverse_events: All 21 categories and numerical values are preserved in Table 3.
source_narrative.weight_change: Mean (SD) weight gain: hydrocortisone 1.5 (1.9) kg versus placebo 0.5 (1.9) kg, P = .02.
source_narrative.adrenal_suppression: Twelve of 33 randomized hydrocortisone patients versus none of 33 placebo patients had suboptimal cosyntropin responses at treatment end, P < .001 by 2-sided Fisher exact test.
source_narrative.severe_response_threshold: Stimulated cortisol <276 nmol/L (<10 µg/dL): 5 patients, all hydrocortisone.
source_narrative.additional_suboptimal_threshold: Stimulated cortisol 276-497 nmol/L (10-18 µg/dL): 7 patients, all hydrocortisone.
source_narrative.withdrawal_harms: One placebo recipient developed a rash; five participants discontinued because of perceived CFS exacerbation, two hydrocortisone and three placebo.
source_narrative.pregnancy: Two women became pregnant during treatment and were considered study completers after 55 and 67 days; treatment allocation not specified in that narrative.
source_narrative.interpretation: Reported symptoms were generally mild, but adrenal suppression was judged clinically important and to preclude practical use for CFS.

reported_discontinuations.note: Perceived CFS worsening versus treatment-emergent adverse reaction classification is unclear; exact all-cause withdrawal reasons retained without assigning causal AE totals.

summary: This 70-person hydrocortisone trial found mixed Wellness results, no significant differences on other rating scales, and adrenal suppression in12/33 active versus0/33 placebo recipients. All three tables, both figures and numerical narrative are retained. Outcome-specific Ns, imputation, multiple comparisons, source discrepancies and safety findings require synthesis review.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: All six pages, three tables and two figures reviewed. Retained all39 baseline,14 clinical-change and22 adverse-reaction rows; corrected Anxiety P to >.99. Recovered eight correlations and the daily Sign test, fixed missing stimulated-cortisol P<.001 and separated treatment, analysis, safety and selected-taper populations.

_extraction_inputs.source_review: All supplied native pages and own-study tables/figures reviewed; prior batch omissions and metadata conflicts reconciled in this source-bound candidate.

_source_findings.reason: Randomized35/35, completed32/31, Wellness30/35, baseline Wellness29/35 and endocrine safety33/33 are distinct. Methods, Table2 imputation footnote and flow withdrawal labels do not fully align. Six-week taper applied only to five active participants; it is not general follow-up.

Table2 Wilcoxon P values are rank-based distribution tests, not mean-difference uncertainty. No multiplicity adjustment; threshold-response counts are not reconstructed from rounded percentages. Source mean-difference/unit discrepancies remain explicit. Adrenal suppression is a biomarker harm, not an inferred serious-event total.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Among those with CFS less than 3 years, 4/15 improved with fludrocortisone versus 0/14 with placebo; no difference was observed.
Among those younger than 30 years, 3/12 improved with fludrocortisone versus 0/9 with placebo; no difference was observed.
Among tolerant and compliant participants, 7/33 (21.2%) improved with fludrocortisone versus 5/43 (11.6%) with placebo.

summary: This double-blind randomized trial tested oral fludrocortisone 0.1 mg/day for 9 weeks in adults with CDC-defined CFS and tilt-test-provoked neurally mediated hypotension. At least a 15-point wellness improvement occurred in 14% of fludrocortisone recipients versus 10% of placebo recipients, with no statistically significant difference (P=.76); other symptom, functional, and tilt-test outcomes were also generally similar.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: All two tables, two figures and full native narrative reviewed. Baseline/flow/harms and subgroup statistics retained. Endpoint N is unreported for most secondary measures; continuous Table2 versus Figure2 counts differ for an explained six-day record. Tilt-test p scope and week2 dose wording remain uncertain. No exact scatterplot coordinates inferred; no synthesis approval.

corrections: Corrected placebo 5-point response from 6/50 to 17/50.
Restricted primary designation to prespecified 15-point response and used ITT N=50 per arm.
Removed unsupported secondary analyzed counts, inferred AE counts and unreported death zeros.
Separated ambiguous tilt-test p value and subgroup comparison from interaction tests.
Preserved reported subgroup estimates and differences in available wellness data.
_prior_source_adjudication.remaining_hold: Unresolved secondary outcome denominators and tilt-test comparison scope.

title: Fludrocortisone Acetate to Treat Neurally Mediated Hypotension in Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
authors: Peter C. Rowe; Hugh Calkins; Karen DeBusk; Robin McKenzie; Ravinder Anand; Geetika Sharma; Brenda A. Cuccherini; Norberto Soto; Patricia Hohman; Sally Snader; Katherine E. Lucas; Mark Wolff; Stephen E. Straus

release_limitations.reason: Source data have been reviewed. Documented source limitations and synthesis decisions still prevent numerical conclusions.

study_design.design_type_detail: parallel-group, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 5-arm trial
study_design.randomization_method: Balanced blocks of 5 patients in a 1:1:1:1:1 ratio using a schedule produced with SAS; the next available lowest randomization number was assigned at each center.

key_inclusion_criteria: Age 18 to 65 years
Modified US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention diagnosis for CFS
Illness duration less than 7 years
key_exclusion_criteria: Major depressive disorder and other specified psychiatric diagnoses
Primary fibromyalgia without concomitant CFS criteria
Participation in cognitive behavioral therapy or graded exercise programs

per_arm.n_randomized_quote: A total of 89 patients were randomly assigned to receive 2.5 mg of galantamine hydrobromide
a total of 82 patients received matching placebo tablets 3 times per day
86 patients, 5.0 mg
91 patients, 7.5 mg
86 patients, 10 mg

sample_sizes.nonmedicated_randomized_note: One2.5mg participant did not receive drug because enrollment closed

source_table1.native_correction: Age final category >50, not >=50; omitted ethnic categories restored. Height5mg is168.8, confirmed in enlarged native crop.

cognitive_normative_comparison.population: CFS patients versus age-matched external CDR normative database; not randomized arms
cognitive_normative_comparison.additional_reference: 329ms among trial patients with group mean ages37–39.1 vs308ms external normative age80–87; external reference is not a trial arm

risk_of_bias.tool: Provisional source-grounded bias appraisal (not a complete RoB 2 assessment)
risk_of_bias.key_concern: Thirty percent withdrew and primary analyses used last observation carried forward, with no arm-specific completion counts reported.

notable_aes.event: Suicide; report states independent safety panel and coroner judged it unrelated to trial medication

overall_reported.attribution: Source judged none attributable to drug; suicide independently judged unrelated by safety panel and coroner

narrative.common_event_scope: Both galantamine and placebo; counts not reported
narrative.higher_dose_trend: More adverse events and withdrawals; no statistically significant group difference reported
narrative.monitoring_rule: BDI rise>=6 or total>=16 required withdrawal

follow_up.schedule: Two-week screening; titration3–8weeks, total16weeks treatment; four-weekly assessments and follow-up four weeks after final dose. Early withdrawals assessed four weeks after last dose and at scheduled week16. Cortisol at baseline/weeks8,12,16, fasting10am±1hour, menstrual days1–7 where applicable.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: US patients exhibited greater improvement than European patients.
Country effects were observed in the total score and many subscales.
A country-by-treatment interaction was observed; largest improvements differed by country and dose.
No statistically significant prognostic influence was found.

summary: This double-blind randomized trial tested four oral doses of galantamine hydrobromide against placebo for 16 weeks in 434 adults with chronic fatigue syndrome. Galantamine did not significantly improve Clinician Global Impression scores or secondary fatigue, function, sleep, quality-of-life, cortisol, or cognitive outcomes compared with placebo; adverse events and withdrawals increased with higher doses.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: All three native tables, two figures, participant flow and numerical narrative reviewed. Corrected high-dose sleep-duration change to−0.13. Table2 descriptive response counts differ from adjusted primary ITT models; Table3 lacks uncertainty and outcome-specific N. Baseline/external cognitive comparisons, pooled safety and country/model findings are retained. Exact plotted values are not inferred. Source age/response statements conflict; synthesis remains held.

study_design.design_type_detail: parallel-group, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 5-arm trial
study_design.randomization_method: Balanced blocks of 5 patients in a 1:1:1:1:1 ratio using a schedule produced with SAS; the next available lowest randomization number was assigned at each center.

key_inclusion_criteria: Age 18 to 65 years
Modified US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention diagnosis for CFS
Illness duration less than 7 years
key_exclusion_criteria: Major depressive disorder and other specified psychiatric diagnoses
Primary fibromyalgia without concomitant CFS criteria
Participation in cognitive behavioral therapy or graded exercise programs

a total of 82 patients received matching placebo tablets 3 times per day

record.summary: This double-blind randomized trial tested four oral doses of galantamine hydrobromide against placebo for 16 weeks in 434 adults with chronic fatigue syndrome. Galantamine did not significantly improve Clinician Global Impression scores or secondary fatigue, function, sleep, quality-of-life, cortisol, or cognitive outcomes compared with placebo; adverse events and withdrawals increased with higher doses.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 contains categorical CGI counts and percentages rather than means and SDs. Table 3 reports least-square mean changes without SDs, SEs, or arm-specific analyzed Ns. The supplied text includes table rows for CGI categories 0-6, but numeric extraction is represented for categories 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6; some table rows are merged/garbled, especially Week 12 and follow-up labels. Numeric values in Figure 2 are not available beyond narrative placebo response rates.

issues.reason: Verified Table 2 category counts yield visit-specific denominators distinct from Figure 1 ITT LOCF/retrieved populations. Derived response counts must not be treated as the adjusted primary ITT result. Table 3 lacks uncertainty estimates and outcome-specific analyzed N; pooling remains held.
Age eligibility18–65 conflicts with maximum67; Discussion placebo response50% conflicts with18.4% at week16. No inferred correction or synthesis approval.

_scientific_validation.note: Numerical checks and quote matches do not establish correct table-column attribution.

_source_harms_summary.note: One randomized participant did not receive study medication.

completion.limitations: All numerical results, tables, figures and source narrative reviewed; reporting ambiguities are preserved. No cited supplement to this trial identified in the supplied report.

summary: This double-blind randomized trial tested low-dose oral clonidine for 9 weeks in 120 adolescents with chronic fatigue syndrome. Clonidine significantly reduced plasma norepinephrine and serum C-reactive protein, but the primary activity outcome favored placebo with a nonsignificant mean difference of −637 steps per day (P = .07), and clonidine was not clinically useful.

Week 8 and week 30 per-arm endpoint values were not reported in the supplied text.

summary: In adults with CFS, 12 weeks of oral ubiquinol-10 at 150 mg/day was compared with placebo in a randomized parallel-group trial. Ubiquinol significantly increased CoQ10 concentrations and improved arithmetic-task responses, nighttime awakenings, and HF power, while fatigue and depression outcomes were not reported numerically at follow-up and were described as not significantly different between groups.

summary: This pilot randomized study tested an 8-week mindfulness-based cognitive therapy program in adults with CFS who continued to experience excessive fatigue after CBT, compared with a waiting list. Adjusted analyses found significantly better MBCT outcomes for fatigue, impairment, beliefs about emotions, self-compassion, catastrophizing, all-or-nothing behaviour, and depression at post-treatment, with significant between-group differences for fatigue, beliefs about emotions, self-compassion, and mindfulness at 2-month follow-up. Improvements in fatigue and several secondary outcomes were maintained in the MBCT group at 6 months.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: The randomization procedure and handling of one lost participant were insufficiently described, and several outcomes were reported primarily through model trajectories or figures.

summary: This double-blind randomized trial assigned 30 adults with CFS and elevated HHV-6/EBV antibody titers to valganciclovir or placebo for 6 months, followed by 6 months of follow-up. Valganciclovir significantly improved trajectories for mental fatigue, fatigue severity, and cognitive functioning, and participants were 7.4 times more likely to be classified as responders; the primary MFI-20 total-score change was not statistically significant.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Several table minus signs are garbled in the supplied text. Most numeric follow-up outcomes are reported as mixed-effects trajectory coefficients rather than raw endpoint means and SDs; several biomarker results are p-values or fold changes only. Safety outcomes are described as assessed but no adverse-event counts are reported.

record.summary: This double-blind randomized trial compared valganciclovir with placebo in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome and serological evidence of reactivated EBV and/or HHV-6 infection. The discussion reports 15 clinical responders, with 13 in the valganciclovir arm and 2 in the placebo arm, but no numerical significance test for this responder comparison is provided in this section.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This source section contains no per-arm means, SDs, sample sizes, confidence intervals, or detailed numeric outcome tables; laboratory trajectories are described as figure-based without extractable numeric values. The responder count of 13 in the VGCV arm is calculated from 15 total responders minus 2 responders not in that arm.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: Only 43 of 60 consented randomized participants provided both samples, and sample provision was strongly associated with subsequent improvement.

follow_up.treatment_duration_weeks_quote: Both treatment conditions involved 12 individual treatment sessions and lasted for between 4 and 6 months.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Memory CD4+ T cells were significantly elevated in patients who did not improve; numerical subgroup means were not reported.

At onset, HLA-DR+ CD8 T cells were 8.2% in improved patients versus 13.6% in those who did not improve; t=2.52, P=0.014. The association disappeared after adjustment for treatment condition, F=1.898, P=0.18.
Baseline HLA-DR+ CD8 T cells were 8.6% in CBT versus 14.2% in relaxation therapy, t=2.48, P=0.02.

summary: This randomized trial compared 12-session cognitive behavior therapy with relaxation therapy in adults meeting Oxford criteria for CFS. Among 43 participants providing paired immune samples, treatment produced no significant changes in lymphocyte subsets; compared with 20 healthy controls, CFS participants had higher natural killer cells and CD11b+ CD8 T cells. Baseline immune measures did not independently predict clinical improvement after adjustment for treatment condition.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Tables 2-4 report pooled CFS participants rather than separate CBT and relaxation-arm means, so arm_results for these laboratory outcomes use arm_id null and identify the CFS or control subgroup in source_location. Tables provide means and SDs but not per-arm randomized or analyzed sample sizes. Clinical outcome instruments and numerical per-arm treatment results were reported elsewhere and are not included in the supplied text. Correlation coefficients and subgroup statistics are reported narratively without compatible arm-level means.

record.summary: This section reports baseline immune-cell measurements in adults with CFS receiving cognitive behavior therapy or relaxation therapy, comparing participants who improved with those who did not. Most immune-cell differences were not statistically significant; activated HLA-DR+ CD8 T cells were higher in unimproved participants (13.6 vs 8.2%, P=0.014).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The supplied section contains Tables 5–7 comparing improved versus unimproved participants, not randomized CBT versus relaxation arms. Therefore subgroup values were preserved in subgroup_analyses rather than incorrectly assigned to intervention arms. Sample sizes for table subgroups and numeric second-sample values are not reported in this section. Correlation statistics were also reported narratively.

summary: This double-blind randomized trial evaluated three months of oral synbiotic supplementation in 26 adults with post-COVID-19 ME/CFS. Synbiotic treatment significantly improved several within-group outcomes, particularly post-exercise malaise, but most reported between-group interaction effects were not statistically significant; the post-exercise malaise interaction favored synbiotic treatment (P=0.02).

The supplied text contains garbled table-footnote placement and an apparent typo stating placebo NAA increase at 12-month follow-up despite a 3-month trial.

record.summary: This parallel-group RCT tested six months of self-paced low-intensity aquatic exercise in adults with ME/CFS. The intervention significantly improved 6-minute walk distance, sit-to-stand performance, fatigue, depression, peak expiratory flow and platelet concentration, with no reported adverse events or worsening of ME/CFS symptoms.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The supplied section contains no numeric per-arm means, SDs, or sample sizes for the outcomes; psychosocial values are presented in figures only. Several pulmonary, functional, hematology and psychosocial outcomes are described narratively without exact effect estimates.

summary: In this double-blind placebo-controlled trial subset, 14 women with fibromyalgia/chronic fatigue syndrome received subcutaneous Staphypan Berna and 14 received sterile-water placebo for 24 weeks. Staphypan Berna significantly increased alpha-toxin, neutralisation, and lipase antibody measures, with reported between-group p-values below 0.001, below 0.001, and below 0.01, respectively. Greater serological responses were correlated with greater clinical improvement.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 3 reports mean values with SEM, not SD, and provides numeric serology only for the active group. Clinical endpoint means and numeric placebo serology values were not reported. Figure 1 contains values only graphically. The paper reports additional correlation coefficients: neutralisation with CPRS-15 r=0.67 post-treatment and r=0.69 pre-treatment, neutralisation with FIQ r=0.57 pre-treatment, weighted antibody response with CPRS-15 r=0.70 and FIQ r=0.67, plus several symptom-level correlations.

Outcomes omitted due to the five-secondary-outcome limit: Age, Gender, Focusing on fatigue, and Perceived problems with activity.

summary: This double-blind randomized trial compared six monthly infusions of IV immunoglobulin G with albumin placebo in 30 adults with chronic fatigue syndrome. Among 28 evaluable participants, IV IgG restored IgG1 levels but did not produce significant clinical benefit in symptoms or functional status; major adverse experiences occurred in 20% of both groups.

summary: This double-blind randomized trial compared three monthly intravenous immunoglobulin infusions with placebo in 49 adults with chronic fatigue syndrome. At 3 months after the final infusion, physician-assessed response occurred in 43% versus 11% of participants, respectively, with a statistically significant between-group difference (p=0.03), although adverse effects were substantially more frequent with immunoglobulin.

summary: This double-blind, randomized 2x2 factorial trial enrolled 90 adults with CFS to receive dialyzable leukocyte extract or placebo, with or without CBT. Neither treatment produced a clinically significant benefit over nonspecific treatment; the combination showed a statistically significant Quality-of-Life improvement, but this was not supported by other outcomes.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table II reports means without arm-level SDs and contains garbled OCR labels and separators. Two participants withdrew and were excluded from analyses: one placebo/clinic and one DLE/clinic. Adverse-event counts were reported only pooled by DLE versus placebo, not by factorial arm. Table I psychiatric morbidity values were extracted conceptually but are not treatment-arm outcomes.

summary: This small double-blind randomized trial tested weekly intramuscular magnesium sulphate for 6 weeks in adults with chronic fatigue syndrome and low red-cell magnesium. Magnesium produced significantly greater improvements than placebo in NHP energy, pain, emotional reactions, and overall scores, while sleep, social isolation, and physical mobility were not statistically significant.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper includes a separate matched case-control study with 20 CFS cases and 20 controls; its red-cell magnesium means were 1.60 versus 1.70 mmol/L, difference 0.10 mmol/L, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.15, p<0.001. Table II does not report SDs or arm-specific analyzed Ns for change scores. Table III reports Group A change data for n=14 because one participant refused blood sampling. The printed overall CI upper bound equals the effect estimate and is preserved verbatim.

record.summary: This small double-blind randomized trial tested weekly intramuscular magnesium sulphate for 6 weeks in adults with chronic fatigue syndrome and low red-cell magnesium. Magnesium produced significantly greater improvements than placebo in NHP energy, pain, emotional reactions, and overall scores, while sleep, social isolation, and physical mobility were not statistically significant.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper includes a separate matched case-control study with 20 CFS cases and 20 controls; its red-cell magnesium means were 1.60 versus 1.70 mmol/L, difference 0.10 mmol/L, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.15, p<0.001. Table II does not report SDs or arm-specific analyzed Ns for change scores. Table III reports Group A change data for n=14 because one participant refused blood sampling. The printed overall CI upper bound equals the effect estimate and is preserved verbatim.

issues.reason: Source Table II emotional change difference does not equal the printed arm changes, and the overall upper CI equals the effect estimate. Participant flow describes two active withdrawals before stating 15/17 randomized. Preserve printed data; primary change denominators and discrepant estimates require synthesis adjudication.
7/11 active participants fell from energy score 100 to 0; 1/14 placebo participants had a reduction, without a reported final score. These are not the same binary endpoint.

_scientific_validation.note: Numerical checks and quote matches do not establish correct table-column attribution.

_source_separate_case_control.design: 20 CFS cases and 20 matched controls, no participant overlap with randomized trial
_source_separate_case_control.synthesis: Etiological comparison; not a randomized treatment effect

summary: In this double-blind randomized crossover trial of 60 adults with chronic fatigue syndrome and concentration difficulties, 4 weeks of oral methylphenidate 10 mg twice daily was compared with placebo. Methylphenidate significantly improved fatigue and concentration, with clinically significant responses in 17% for fatigue and 22% for concentration; benefits were also observed for SF-36 physical factor and vitality.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Full-context Luna extraction plus compact Luna completion of both tables. All 27 Table 1 rows, four Table 2 physiological measures, six symptom rows, all reported within-person contrasts, and two clinical responder outcomes retained after native-source review.

record.summary: In this double-blind randomized crossover trial of 60 adults with chronic fatigue syndrome and concentration difficulties, 4 weeks of oral methylphenidate 10 mg twice daily was compared with placebo. Methylphenidate significantly improved fatigue and concentration, with clinically significant responses in 17% for fatigue and 22% for concentration; benefits were also observed for SF-36 physical factor and vitality.

summary: This randomized trial tested one 30-minute pain physiology education session versus pacing and self-management education in adults with chronic fatigue syndrome and chronic widespread pain. Pain physiology education significantly improved pain neurophysiology knowledge (P < .001; Cohen d = 2.53) and reduced rumination (P = .009); reported arm-level means and SDs were not included in the supplied text.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 and Figure 2 are referenced but Table 2 numeric values are absent from the supplied text; outcome values shown only in the unavailable table/figures were not reconstructed. The paper states additional Cohen d values ranging from .79 to 2.53 but does not assign them individually in the supplied text.

record.summary: This parallel-group randomized trial compared a single session of pain physiology education with pacing and self-management education in adults with chronic fatigue syndrome and chronic widespread pain. Pain physiology education substantially improved neurophysiology pain knowledge and reduced rumination, while effects on mean pressure pain threshold were minimal.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Numeric results were extracted from Table 2. The table reports before, after, absolute difference, and Cohen d values but does not report sample sizes or confidence intervals. Cohen d values appear in the control rows and were treated as between-group effects; standardization was not specified.

summary: This double-blind randomized trial assigned 30 adults with post-COVID asthenic syndrome to 10 days of intramuscular CCSA or placebo. CCSA produced larger reported improvements in MFI-20 fatigue scores (20 versus 12 points; p=0.043) and MoCA scores (2 versus 1 point; p<0.05), although SDs and analyzed Ns were not reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The supplied text reports clinical outcomes only as between-arm change values without SDs or outcome-specific Ns. MRI tables report T statistics, corrected or uncorrected p-values, voxel counts, and coordinates but do not provide means, SDs, or between-arm effect estimates. Table 7 is referenced but its contents are absent from the supplied text.

within_group_tests.effect_quote: At 24 month follow-up, no signi fi cant group difference was found in the proportion of either adolescents ' or mothers ' reports that the adolescent was much better or very much better overall (Fisher ' s exact test ¼ 0.62 and 1.00 respectively). McNemar tests indicated that there was no signi fi cant change in either group in the proportion of adolescents or mothers reporting this outcome between six month and 24-month follow-up. In the adolescents in the psycho-education group, the proportion was 89% at 24 month follow-up, compared with 70% at 6-month follow-up ( p ¼ 1.00). The corresponding ratings for mothers in the psycho-education group were 90% and 75% ( p ¼ 0.50). In the CBT group 77% of adolescents reported being much or very much better at 24 month follow-up, compared to 83% at six-month follow-up ( p ¼ 0.63). For mothers in the CBT group the corresponding fi gures were 94% and 72% ( p ¼ 0.50).

study_identity_evidence.source_quote: The results of a randomised controlled trial comparing familyfocused CBT with psycho-education were previously reported (Chalder, Deary, Husain, & Walwyn, 2010). This was one of only three RCTs (Chalder et al., 2010; Nijhof, Bleijenberg, Ulterwaal, Kimpen, & van de Putte, 2012; Stulemeijer, de Jong, Fiselier & Bleijenberg, 2005) investigating the effectiveness of CBT in adolescents, but the only one to compare CBT with another active treatment. Whilst adolescents receiving family-focused CBT were found to have greater improvement in school attendance at end of treatment than those receiving psycho-education, at six month follow-up both groups had improved to the same extent.

summary: This two-arm feasibility RCT tested 12 sessions of fatigue-focused CBM-I versus matched control training in 131 adults with long-term health conditions, including chronic fatigue syndrome and post-COVID condition. record.summary: This two-arm feasibility RCT tested four weeks of fatigue-focused online CBM-I/FLEX against matched control training in adults with long-term health conditions and high fatigue. FLEX produced a large post-intervention improvement in fatigue-related interpretation bias (Hedges' g=0.834) and small effects on several self-reported outcomes; no significance tests were performed.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: A randomization error led to removal of male subjects and unequal analyzed placebo and intervention samples.

summary: This double-blind randomized trial tested a single 60-mg oral dose of pyridostigmine in adults with ME/CFS undergoing serial invasive cardiopulmonary exercise testing. Compared with placebo, pyridostigmine significantly improved peak VO2 and peak-rest VO2, cardiac output, right atrial pressure, and Borg fatigue scores, although several secondary outcomes had no significant between-group difference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper reports 45 randomized participants, but six participants were excluded from analysis after a randomization error involving male subjects; Table 1 and Table 2 therefore use pyridostigmine n=23 and placebo n=16. Treatment-effect confidence intervals appear directionally inconsistent with the reported positive effect estimates and were transcribed verbatim.

source_design_and_timing.design: Proof-of-concept, randomized, controlled, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial
source_design_and_timing.site: CFS Clinical Unit, Vall d'Hebron University Hospital, Barcelona, Spain

eligibility.diagnosis: CFS according to 1994 CDC case criteria

questionnaires.pain: 15-item McGill Pain Questionnaire; sensory 11 items and affective 4 items
questionnaires.sleep: 24-item Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index; seven components, global range 0–21

key_inclusion_criteria: female sex
age 18 to 65 years
confirmed chronic fatigue syndrome diagnosis according to 1994 CDC case criteria
resting radial pulse 50 to 100 bpm
systolic blood pressure 100 to 140 mmHg
diastolic blood pressure 50 to 90 mmHg
key_exclusion_criteria: participation in another trial within 30 days
use of prohibited drugs or supplements
hepatobiliary tract disease affecting CoQ10 bioavailability
cardiovascular or pulmonary disorder interfering with maximal exercise testing
inability to comply with study requirements

source_figures.description: Bar chart of change in maximum HR from baseline to week 8 for CoQ10 + NADH and placebo, with error bars and bracket annotation.

printed_values.interpretation: More negative scores indicate greater diminution of maximum HR from baseline.

plot_only_fields_unavailable: Exact bar heights and error-bar endpoints cannot be recovered from the plot without guessing.

all_numerical_narrative.result: Active-group maximum HR decreased at week 8 versus baseline: 136.8 ± 14.2 versus 140.1 ± 15.3 bpm, P=0.022.
Between-group max-HR change was not statistically significant: CoQ10 + NADH −3.28 ± 8.7 versus placebo −1.82 ± 12.2; F=3.53; P-trend=0.225.
No between-group differences in change in VO2, VCO2, maximal workload, respiratory quotient, arm systolic BP or arm diastolic BP; P>0.05 for each.
Borg-score change did not differ: active 0.25 ± 1.35 versus placebo 0.12 ± 1.63; F=0.15; P=0.66.

Active-group FIS total scores decreased from baseline at week 4 and week 8, P=0.021 and P=0.03. Placebo-group FIS total score also differed from baseline at week 4, P=0.04, but not reported as significant at week 8.
FIS total and physical, cognitive and psychosocial subscore changes did not differ significantly between groups at weeks 4 or 8; Table 3 gives all contrasts.

The narrative describes placebo sensory and affective pain reductions using 21.8 ± 6.0 to 17.7 ± 7.4 and 8.9 ± 3.1 to 6.8 ± 3.6, each P=.01. Table 3 instead locates 21.8 and 8.9 in the active week-8 column; placebo baseline values are 22.1 and 8.8. Preserve the contradiction.
Week-8 treatment effects favored placebo for sensory pain: placebo −4.35 ± 7.5 versus active 1.59 ± 6.4, P=0.002; and affective pain: placebo −1.94 ± 3.8 versus active 0.41 ± 3.7, P=0.006.
At week 8 active participants had fewer sleep disturbances: F=3.83, P<0.001, and greater hypnotic-medication-use score: F=−2.75, P=0.008. Table 4 reports the corresponding values and contrasts.
Week-8 PBMC levels differed: CoQ10 active 361.8 ± 37 versus placebo 155.1 ± 26 pmole/mg proteins, P<0.05; NADH active 247.3 ± 5.1 versus placebo 98.2 ± 4.6 pmole/106 PBMC, P<0.001.

Authors characterize CoQ10 + NADH as generally safe and well tolerated and potentially useful for max HR and perceived fatigue, while stating no positive between-group effect on pain or sleep disturbances.

summary: This 80-person randomized trial reports no significant between-group change in its primary maximum-heart-rate outcome or fatigue scores. summary: This single-center randomized trial compared 8 weeks of Prolong Life With Nine Turn Method Qigong with cognitive behavioral therapy in adults with Fukuda-defined chronic fatigue syndrome. Both groups improved MFI-20 fatigue scores, and the 8-week between-group difference was not statistically significant (mean difference −2.50, 95% CI −7.74 to 2.74; p=0.346).

The supplement contains the movement illustration only. Printed contrast direction and postrandomization exclusions remain unresolved for synthesis.

study_design.design_type_detail: parallel-group, two-arm randomized open-label active-controlled pilot study
study_design.randomization_method: Randomization was based on the enrollment list; even-numbered subjects received amisulpride, with subject order casually generated by an observer blinded to the study design.

design_labels: Authors also characterize it as observational and un-blinded
source_design_and_timing.setting: Single center; referrals from treating clinicians and self-referrals.
source_design_and_timing.population: Non-depressed CFS patients meeting published Fukuda criteria; no neurological or psychiatric comorbidity reported.
source_design_and_timing.allocation: After enrollment, subjects were randomized; even-numbered enrollment-list subjects received amisulpride. Enrollment-list order was described as casually generated by an observer blinded to the study design.
source_design_and_timing.blinding: Subjects were aware of treatment and all were un-blinded to regimen. Clinician assessing CGI-S was blinded to drug regimen. The observer generating enrollment-list order was described as blinded to study design.
source_design_and_timing.primary_outcome: Symptom alleviation after 12 weeks, measured by standardized self-reports, pain scales, and clinician evaluation.
source_design_and_timing.registration: Not registered in international clinical-trial databases.

instruments.FSS: Nine-item self-report fatigue scale; each item rated 1 to 7, where 1 indicates no fatigue-related impairment and 7 severe impairment.
instruments.HADS: Anxiety and depression subscales; cognitive rather than somatic mood/anxiety assessment. HADS-A and HADS-D are each scored below 7 in all enrolled subjects and described as within normal range.
instruments.VAS-pain: 0=no pain or bodily discomfort; 100=maximum pain or bodily discomfort.
instruments.SF-12: Higher scores indicate higher perceived quality of life.
instruments.FIBSER: Frequency, intensity, and global burden of side effects; 7-point domains, higher scores indicate greater side-effect impact.
instruments.CGI-S: Clinician-rated illness severity, scale 1 to 7; higher scores indicate greater severity.

source_dose_and_delivery.administration: Oral regimen implied by tablet dosing terminology but route was not explicitly stated.
source_dose_and_delivery.dose_context: Introduction describes low-dose amisulpride as 100 mg/die or less; the assigned regimen was 25 mg bid.
source_dose_and_delivery.washout_or_carryover: Not applicable to the reported parallel design; no washout or carryover information reported.
source_dose_and_delivery.concomitant_medications: No psychoactive drug use during the six months preceding enrollment; other concomitant-treatment details not reported.

study_design.blinding_detail: Participants unblinded; CGI-S clinician blinded to drug regimen. Observational label and randomization description both retained.

summary: This40-person pilot compared amisulpride with fluoxetine for12weeks. All17 table rows and29 reported tests are retained. Participants were unblinded but the CGI-S clinician was blinded. Table/narrative depression values and overall/arm mean ages conflict; arm-specific analysis denominators and adverse-event counts are unreported.

study_design.design_type_detail: 12-week randomized active-comparator phase followed by12-week agomelatine extension for both original groups
study_design.randomization_method: An electronically generated list of random numbers was consecutively assigned; even numbers were assigned to agomelatine and odd numbers to melatonin.

source_design_and_timing.design: Randomized active-comparator study: double-blind12-week phaseI followed by12weeks with both original groups receiving agomelatine; phaseII treatment blinding unreported.
source_design_and_timing.population: Adults with CFS diagnosed according to Fukuda criteria.
source_design_and_timing.phase_II: Additional 12 weeks, from week 12 to week 24.
source_design_and_timing.randomization: Electronically generated random-number list; numbers assigned consecutively by enrollment order. Even numbers assigned to agomelatine and odd numbers to melatonin. Labels were stored in closed envelopes until screening completion.
source_design_and_timing.blinding: Patients and evaluating physicians were blinded during phase I; drugs were matched in appearance. CGI-S clinician was blinded to self-report results.
source_design_and_timing.comparator: Sustained-release melatonin, intended as an active comparator for melatonin-receptor agonism.
source_design_and_timing.carryover: No formal carryover assessment reported; phase II followed directly after phase I and involved switching the melatonin group to agomelatine.

source_dose_and_delivery.agomelatine: 50 mg/day, phase I; continued through phase II for the originally assigned agomelatine group.
source_dose_and_delivery.switch: All melatonin-treated subjects were switched to agomelatine at week 12 and evaluated at week 24.
source_dose_and_delivery.delivery_details: Route, formulation details beyond sustained release for melatonin, adherence, dose adjustments, and treatment interruptions were not reported.

record.summary: This double-blind randomized trial evaluated 8 weeks of oral Sipjeondaebo-tang granules in adults with CDC-defined chronic fatigue syndrome. summary: This report analyzed 151 fatigued employees on sick leave who had participated in a randomized trial of brief GP-delivered CBT versus usual GP care. At 12 months, 43% were no longer fatigue cases, 62% had resumed work, and 20% met CFS-like criteria; CBT itself was reported elsewhere as having no detectable effect on fatigue or absenteeism. Predictors differed by outcome and baseline CFS-like status.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper is a predictor analysis and does not report treatment-arm-specific outcome means, SDs, or Ns. Table 1 numeric columns are CFS+ and CFS- baseline subgroups, while Table 2 reports total-group and baseline-CFS subgroup counts. The outcome arm_results preserve these reported subgroup/total values using the available two arm slots; they should not be interpreted as CBT-versus-usual-care results. Table 3 odds ratios and GEE odds ratios are reported but not fully represented as separate compact outcome objects because they are model-based predictor effects rather than treatment-arm contrasts.

summary: This pilot randomized trial tested 12 weeks of group cognitive behavioral stress management versus a single psychoeducation seminar in adults with physician-diagnosed CFS. CBSM significantly improved perceived stress, mood disturbance, quality-of-life measures, and total symptom severity compared with control, while fatigue improvement was marginal and symptom frequency was not significant.

summary: This randomized trial tested 16 sessions of cognitive behavior therapy over 8 months in adults with chronic fatigue syndrome, compared with nondirective counseling or no intervention. CBT significantly reduced focusing on fatigue more than control and this change mediated improvements in fatigue severity and impairment; avoidance behaviors did not differ significantly between groups.

summary: This reanalysis examined a low-intensity cognitive behavioral intervention delivered by written self-instructions and e-mail in adults with chronic fatigue syndrome, compared with a waiting list. Among 139 complete cases, treatment effects on fatigue and disability were mediated by reduced perceived problems with activity and increased sense of control over fatigue. Treatment did not significantly change focus on symptoms; detailed per-arm outcome means and SDs were not reported in the supplied text.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 1 reports baseline means and SDs for included versus excluded participants, not separately by randomized treatment arm. Numeric model results are largely figure-only: standardized effects are shown in Figs. 2-3 without extractable values in the supplied text. Explicit numeric model details include 73% of the treatment effect on fatigue explained by mediators, 75% for physical functioning, MI=8.3 for both mediator directions, and MI=22.9 versus 18.2 for the physical-functioning-to-fatigue direction. Table 1 also reports Wilks-Lambda=.97, F=.82, p=.560 for the multivariate exclusion comparison.

Among 139 complete cases, standardized mediation effects were reported for fatigue, physical functioning, and overall impairment, with statistically significant mediated proportions generally ranging from 21% to 75%.

summary: This secondary analysis combined two randomized trials of guided self-instruction versus wait list in 261 adults meeting CDC criteria for CFS. Guided self-instruction produced greater clinically significant fatigue improvement, particularly among patients without clinically relevant depressive symptoms and those with lower activity avoidance; age, depression, and activity avoidance moderated continuous fatigue response.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper is a secondary moderator analysis and does not report post-treatment per-arm continuous means or SDs. Focus-on-bodily-symptoms data were unavailable from the tertiary-centre trial. Numerical subgroup results for avoidance of activity were only in Figure 1. The stated six-month wait period was used for total duration.

summary: This four-arm randomized trial evaluated adaptive pacing therapy, cognitive behavioural therapy, and graded exercise therapy, each combined with specialist medical care, versus specialist medical care alone in 641 adults with CFS. record.summary: This section reports adverse events and deterioration through 52 weeks in adults with CFS randomized to CBT, SMC, GET, or APT. Serious adverse events, serious adverse reactions, fatigue deterioration, combined function/fatigue deterioration, and CGI deterioration did not differ significantly between arms, whereas physical-function deterioration differed significantly (P=.0007), being highest with APT. Baseline depressive and CFS symptom burden were associated with greater NSAE counts.

summary: This secondary analysis of the four-arm PACE randomized trial examined complementary and alternative medicine use among 640 adults with CFS. CAM use was common, but treatment-arm differences at 52 weeks were not statistically significant; baseline CAM use was associated with a small, statistically significant improvement in SF-36 physical function that was below the clinically important threshold.

Table 5 is referenced but not reproduced; only the SF-36 effect reported in the abstract and narrative was extractable.

record.summary: This secondary analysis examined associations between complementary and alternative medicine use and outcomes among adults with CFS in the four-arm PACE trial. Baseline CAM use was associated with higher SF-36 scores, but most fatigue and SF-36 associations were not statistically significant; the study reported no clinically important overall improvement associated with CAM use.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Source section contains Table 5 model-adjusted mean differences for CAM-use exposure groups, but no per-arm raw means, SDs, or analyzed Ns. Table 5 reports original p-values; the footnote states Bonferroni-adjusted p-values of 0.054 for Any CAM use at baseline and 0.024 for CAM medication use at baseline. CAM exposure comparisons are not the four randomized treatment-arm comparisons.

record.summary: This randomized pilot trial compared heart rate variability biofeedback with graded exercise training in adults with chronic fatigue syndrome. Both groups showed reductions in fatigue, while biofeedback significantly improved mental quality of life and depression and graded exercise significantly improved physical quality of life; between-group differences favored biofeedback for mental quality of life and depression.

summary: This two-arm randomized trial evaluated guided graded exercise self-help added to specialist medical care in adults with chronic fatigue syndrome. GES improved fatigue more than specialist medical care at 12 weeks, but the difference was not maintained at long-term follow-up; physical functioning also showed no significant long-term difference. Healthcare costs were £85 higher with GES, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of £4,802 per QALY.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 1 reports characteristics by follow-up participation rather than randomized arm and therefore was not mapped into per-arm demographics. Long-term follow-up was reported as a median of 15 months with IQR 13-19 and range 11-36 months. The supplied text does not provide arm-specific randomization totals, adverse-event data, CGI numerical results, QALY differences, or confidence intervals for costs.

record.summary: This double-blind randomized trial tested intermittent oral high-dose vitamin D3 for six months in adults with Fukuda- and Canadian-criteria CFS/ME and low vitamin D levels. Vitamin D significantly increased 25OHD and reduced PTH at six months, but did not significantly improve vascular, inflammatory, oxidative-stress, metabolic, or fatigue outcomes overall.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Only the supplied source body.md section was used. Sample sizes and baseline demographic values were not reported in this section. Table 4 contains merged and misordered cells; some LDL, HDL, triglyceride, and HOMA-IR timepoint associations are therefore uncertain. Negative signs appear as garbled null-like characters in the supplied text.

summary: This four-arm randomized trial assigned adults with ME/CFS to cognitive behavior therapy, anaerobic activity alone, cognitive coping skills, or relaxation. In a post hoc analysis, participants who stayed within their energy envelope had lower Energy Quotient scores and significant improvements in physical functioning and fatigue severity over time, whereas those exceeding their envelope did not; interaction effects were statistically significant.

The reported outcome analyses compare post-randomization energy-envelope categories rather than the four randomized treatment arms. Exact per-arm randomized sample sizes were reported only as 28–29 per condition.

summary: In this double-blind randomized trial, adults with Fukuda-defined CFS and clinically significant executive-function deficits received flexible-dose oral lisdexamfetamine or placebo for 6 weeks. Lisdexamfetamine produced significantly greater improvement in the BRIEF-A Global Executive Composite and most subscales, with reported effect sizes from 0.62 to 1.57; fatigue and generalized pain were also reported as improved, but their numeric results were not provided in the text.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Numeric values for fatigue, pain, global functioning, anxiety, and safety measures were not reported in the supplied text and figures were unavailable. Table 1 reports change-from-baseline values only. The Shift placebo value contains a garbled minus-sign character in the supplied text.

statistical_methods.power: Enrollment of 60 was estimated to provide at least 64% power for a moderate effect size of 0.60, based on a two-sample t-test with one observation per subject.
statistical_methods.primary_model: Linear mixed regression with treatment, time, and treatment-by-time predictors; random intercepts and slopes; correlated errors; covariance selected among compound symmetry, autoregressive, and antedependence using corrected Akaike information criterion.
statistical_methods.transformations: Log transformations used when appropriate to improve linearity, normalize data, and stabilize variance.
statistical_methods.secondary_analysis: Baseline-to-endpoint change using last observation carried forward; two-sample t-test or Wilcoxon rank-sum test.
statistical_methods.hypothesis_testing: Two-sided; primary type-I error controlled at 0.05; no multiplicity adjustment for secondary measures.
statistical_methods.analysis_population: Modified intent-to-treat: randomized participants with at least one compliant postbaseline visit; compliance defined as taking 80%–120% of study medication by drug accountability.
statistical_methods.model_estimate_warning: Three Table 2 estimates are ratios of relative continuous-score changes: BPI average pain severity, BPI average pain interference, and HADS depression. They are not event-rate ratios.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: Randomization and allocation concealment procedures were not reported, and withdrawals were substantially greater with duloxetine than placebo.

notable_aes.source_location: Safety narrative; serious AE leading to discontinuation

adverse_events.table_selection: Table4 lists events reported by at least5% of duloxetine patients; it is not a complete listing of all events in both arms.

source_table4.caption: Most Frequently Reported Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events
footnotes: Values are number (%) of affected patients; events shown were reported by at least 5% of duloxetine patients.
One duloxetine patient did not have postbaseline data.
Nausea: P ≤ 0.001 versus placebo; somnolence: P ≤ 0.01; dizziness, headache, and dry mouth: P ≤ 0.05.

source_narrative.overall: Most treatment-emergent adverse events were mild to moderate. No clinically important laboratory or physical-examination findings and no significant between-group differences in weight change or vital signs.
source_narrative.serious_adverse_event: One duloxetine patient experienced suicidal ideation, assessed as serious and possibly treatment-related; no suicidal behavior or hospitalization; resolved after discontinuation.
source_narrative.table_4_coverage: 29 adverse-event rows; events were those reported by at least 5% of duloxetine patients.
source_narrative.no_inference: Zeros in Table 4 are reported table values and are not interpreted as absence of all other harms.

summary: In this 60-participant randomized trial, duloxetine did not significantly improve the primary general-fatigue outcome versus placebo. Secondary mental-fatigue and pain findings were exploratory without multiplicity adjustment. Different efficacy, endpoint and safety populations are retained, as are source ambiguity in PGI-I and a bodily-pain CI/P discrepancy. No synthesis approval is implied.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The supplied text ends during the Results section and does not include Tables 1-2, Figure 2-3 numeric values, or the remainder of the efficacy and adverse-event results. Therefore, per-arm means, SDs, and most numerical outcome results are unavailable.

_source_findings.reason: Continuous-score ratio of within-arm relative changes; not an incidence rate ratio, risk ratio or mean difference. Preserve outside supported pooled effect types.

Original Table3 bodily-pain 95% CI includes zero while P=.04. Methods allows t or Wilcoxon tests without mapping each outcome; retain printed results and do not reconstruct uncertainty from P.

Table2 labels observed changes, but PGI-I is first assessed after week1 and positive3.2/3.3 values appear to be endpoint ratings. No pretreatment baseline is reported. Preserve printed values and withhold this outcome from pooling.
Table1 and Table4 footnotes were omitted by conversion and Table2 placebo header truncated. Original PDF page texts are preserved here; all affected counts checked against PDF.
Original Table1 prints HADS range0-7 while several means exceed7. Retained original table and avoided treating this range as a validated measurement limit.
Original Table1 range0-7 conflicts with reported means exceeding7. Numeric scores retained; range is not used to normalize outcomes.

Native Table 2 pain-severity ratio .73 (.54,1.00), P=.05 and CGI-S difference -.1 (-.3,0.0), P=.02 have rounded bounds touching their null. Table 3 bodily-pain CI/P differs as already noted. group [10%] and 0 in the placebo group; P ¼ 0.24 using

adverse event and possibly related to duloxetine
treatment. The patient did not have any suicidal
behavior and did not require hospitalization. The
ideation resolved after discontinuation of duloxetine.
Other adverse events associated with discontinuation
in the duloxetine-treated patients included somnolence
(n ¼ 1) and constipation (n ¼ 1). Duloxetine-treated
patients reported nausea, somnolence, dizziness, and
dry mouth signiﬁcantly more frequently than placebo-
treated patients did. Headache was reported by sig-
niﬁcantly more placebo-treated patients than those on
duloxetine (Table 4). There were no signiﬁcant differ-
ences in weight change or vital signs between dulox-
etine- and placebo-treated patients from baseline to
endpoint. Most treatment-emergent adverse events
were mild to moderate in severity. There were no
clinically important ﬁndings in the laboratory results
or physical examinations.

CFS, improvement in the duloxetine group on the
MFI general fatigue score, which was selected as the
primary measure of fatigue, was not signiﬁcantly
greater than in the placebo group. The duloxetine
group showed signiﬁcantly greater improvement than
the placebo group on the MFI mental fatigue score.
The MFI provides in-depth information across 5
domains of fatigue, each of which has been validated
against a single global fatigue question, supporting the
notion that fatigue is multidimensional and that
different aspects of fatigue should be measured sep-
arately.23 Because patients with CFS often report
fatigue symptoms that are physical and mental in
nature, using the MFI allowed us to examine the effect
of duloxetine across several dimensions of fatigue. The
results of this trial provide preliminary evidence that
duloxetine may result in relief of some dimensions of
fatigue in patients with CFS.
In trials of duloxetine in patients with ﬁbromyal-
gia, a disorder that has overlapping features with
CFS,4 the efﬁcacy of duloxetine vs placebo on
improvement in secondary measures of fatigue, as
measured by the MFI, has been inconsistent.24–26 The
reasons for the inconsistent effect of duloxetine on
speciﬁc domains of fatigue as measured by the MFI in
ﬁbromyalgia trials are unclear but may be related to
differences in individual study design or possible
differential effects of duloxetine on dimensions of
fatigue. Notably, improvement in the MFI mental
fatigue score was a consistent ﬁnding across the
duloxetine ﬁbromyalgia trials and is similar to the
signiﬁcant improvement in mental fatigue in patients
with CFS in the present study.
Duloxetine was also signiﬁcantly superior to
placebo on secondary efﬁcacy measures of pain
including the Brief Pain Inventory average pain
severity and average pain interference scores and the
SF-36 bodily pain domain. In addition, the Clinical
Global Impression of Severity score was signiﬁcantly
improved in the duloxetine group compared with the
placebo group. The efﬁcacy of duloxetine on symp-
toms of pain associated with CFS is consistent with its
