known efﬁcacy in several chronic pain disorders:
duloxetine is approved by the US Food and Drug
Administration for the management of pain associated
with diabetic peripheral neuropathy, management of
chronic musculoskeletal pain, and management of
ﬁbromyalgia.27 Dysfunction of serotonin and norepi-
nephrine transmission, which mediate endogenous
analgesic mechanisms via the descending inhibitory
pain pathways in the central nervous system, may play
a key role in pain symptoms associated with several
chronic pain disorders.28 Emerging evidence suggests
that changes in descending modulatory pathways may
also be involved in the development of chronic pain
associated with CFS.29,30 Duloxetine is hypothesized
to reduce pain symptoms associated with CFS and
chronic pain disorders by increasing serotonin and
norepinephrine neurotransmission in the descending
pain inhibitory pathways.
Although the MFI has been validated in a US
population of individuals with chronic fatigue, there is
no consensus on the outcome measures for fatigue or
other symptom domains in trials of CFS treatments.13 In
addition, there are limited data on the responsiveness to
change of the MFI in clinical trials of patients with CFS
and questions about the dimensional structure of the
scale.31 Reeves et al. used the MFI as part of a battery of
instruments to assess the major dimensions of the CFS,
as speciﬁed by the 1994 case deﬁnition.14 They deﬁned
severe fatigue as a score Z13 on the general fatigue score
of the MFI, which was adopted in the present study as
part of the inclusion criteria. We also included 2 other
measures identiﬁed by Reeves et al. to assess functional
impairment in patients with CFS (SF-36) and deﬁne the
symptom complex associated with CFS (CDC Symp-
tom Inventory).14 It is possible that other measures of
fatigue and function may be preferable for use as
outcomes in CFS clinical trials. A review of the
interventions for CFS identiﬁed many different out-
comes and a variety of scales used to assess symptoms of
CFS.32 The lack of consistency in the use of outcomes
has hindered meaningful comparison of treatments.
There is a need to develop standard outcome measures
for use in trials evaluating treatments for CFS.32
Most patients with CFS tolerated duloxetine, with
most reporting adverse events as mild to moderate
in severity. Signiﬁcantly more duloxetine-treated
patients than placebo-treated patients reported nau-
sea, somnolence, dizziness, and dry mouth. There were
no signiﬁcant differences between treatment groups in
the number of patients who discontinued participation
in the study because of treatment-emergent adverse
events. One patient in the duloxetine group experi-
enced a serious adverse event of suicidal ideation,
which was assessed as being possibly related to
duloxetine. Increased risk of suicidality may occur
with the use of any antidepressant, including dulox-
etine.33 Patients starting treatment with antidepres-
sants for any reason should be informed of this risk
and carefully observed for the emergence of suicidal
thoughts or behaviors during treatment.
The safety ﬁndings in the present study are gen-
erally consistent with the ﬁndings in trials of duloxetine
in patients with ﬁbromyalgia.34 However, the report of

authors: Lesley M. Arnold; Thomas J. Blom; Jeffrey A. Welge; Elizabeth Mariutto; Alicia Heller

release_limitations.reason: Source data have been reviewed. Documented source limitations and synthesis decisions still prevent numerical conclusions.

study_design.design_type_detail: Ancillary observational biomarker analyses nested in a randomized crossover trial; no randomized treatment contrast is reported here.

participants.long_covid_definition: PCC patients met the same adjusted CDC fatigue criteria and showed SARS-CoV-2 seropositivity during screening or a previous hospital visit
required_symptoms: Severe fatigue for at least six months
Unrefreshing sleep and PEM for ME/CFS, QFS and PCC
At least two additional adjusted CDC symptoms for the fatigue-syndrome groups
key_inclusion_criteria: Age 12-29 years
Severe fatigue for at least six months
ME/CFS, QFS, or PCC patients met adjusted CDC criteria
JIA patients met ILAR criteria and had stable disease activity
CIS-8 score >39 for ME/CFS, QFS, and PCC or >34 for JIA
key_exclusion_criteria: Additional diagnosis that could fully explain severe fatigue
Medication use known to interfere with hair cortisol concentration
participants.diagnostic_criteria_note: Adjusted Fukuda/CDC: unrefreshing sleep and PEM required, plus at least two of six other symptoms; half the ME/CFS group also met CCC. QFS/PCC had the same fatigue criteria plus infection attribution. JIA is a distinct rheumatic diagnosis.

sample_sizes.allocation_note: Diagnostic groups and healthy controls were not randomized arms. This report describes 59 included patients, not an explicit randomization total. Parent RCT extraction is separate.

source_power_context.note: Design assumptions and posthoc power, not achieved enrollment or treatment effects.

footnotes: QFS = Q fever Fatigue Syndrome; ME/CFS = Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome; PCC = Post-COVID-19 Condition; JIA = Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis.

Group differences were tested for significance in the last column (group dif. sig.). Continuous variables were tested using one-way univariate ANOVAs, whereas categorical variables were tested using chi-square tests. All analyses and post-hoc comparisons were corrected for multiple testing (Bonferroni). Ns = not significant, ** p < .001, * p < .05.

record.summary: This study examined hair cortisol concentration in adolescents and young adults with ME/CFS, QFS, PCC, JIA, and controls participating in a lifestyle and dietary self-management crossover trial. Baseline HCC was significantly lower in ME/CFS and QFS than in controls, while HCC increased during the trial regardless of clinically relevant fatigue improvement.

results: Baseline maximal power: NADH 74,8 W (SD=43,3), placebo 73,2 W (SD=31,6), p=0,90.
At 60 days, maximal power increased by 3,07 W with NADH and 2,68 W with placebo.
Baseline maximal heart rate: NADH 127/min (SD=23), placebo 123/min (SD=20), p=0,60.
At 60 days, maximal heart rate decreased by 8,2/min with NADH (p<0,05) and increased by 1,7/min with placebo (p=0,73).
NADH baseline maximal-heart-rate/theoretical-maximal-heart-rate was 73% (SD=14%); 60-day difference was -4,2 points (p<0,05).
Placebo baseline ratio was 72% (SD=12%); 60-day difference was 0,66 points (p=0,82).
No statistically significant differences were observed for theoretical VO2max, VO2max, maximal power, blood lactate, or VO2max/theoretical VO2max.

reported_results.note: Baseline SD explicitly labeled DE; changes are within-group, with no change SD or treatment-effect CI.

outcomes.name: Theoretical maximum oxygen uptake
outcomes.synthesis_population: Adults with chronic fatigue syndrome

reported_results.result: No statistically significant difference reported; exact values, uncertainties and P unavailable.

results: Baseline maximal power: NADH 74,8 W (SD=43,3), placebo 73,2 W (SD=31,6), p=0,90.
At 60 days, maximal power increased by 3,07 W with NADH and 2,68 W with placebo.
Baseline maximal heart rate: NADH 127/min (SD=23), placebo 123/min (SD=20), p=0,60.
At 60 days, maximal heart rate decreased by 8,2/min with NADH (p<0,05) and increased by 1,7/min with placebo (p=0,73).
NADH baseline maximal-heart-rate/theoretical-maximal-heart-rate was 73% (SD=14%); 60-day difference was -4,2 points (p<0,05).
Placebo baseline ratio was 72% (SD=12%); 60-day difference was 0,66 points (p=0,82).
No statistically significant differences were observed for theoretical VO2max, VO2max, maximal power, blood lactate, or VO2max/theoretical VO2max.

source_limitations: Only the five-page report identified by DOI 10.1016/j.rce.2009.09.015 was included; publisher cover material and neighboring content were excluded.
No supplementary appendix, statistical analysis plan, trial registry entry, protocol, or companion report was provided.
No confidence intervals, exact test statistics, or complete between-group change estimates were reported.
No arm-specific withdrawals, adherence, protocol deviations, or missingness counts were reported.
No exact denominators were provided for percentage-based efficacy ratings.
No detailed safety-test denominators or complete adverse-event categories were provided.
Figure coordinates beyond printed annotations are unavailable.
No subgroup or adjusted model analyses were reported.
The report does not establish biomarker efficacy; laboratory tests were described only as normal-range safety or clinical assessments.
source_contradictions: Abstract reports maximal heart-rate change as -8,1 l/min with NADH; main text reports -8,2 l/min.
Abstract says 20 mg oral NADH or placebo for the first 2 months; methods additionally specify 5 mg tablets, four daily, for 80 days.
Methods state intention-to-treat with LOCF, while Results state that data from 77 completers were analyzed.
The text reports a depression change of -1,0 in NADH and -0,6 in placebo while describing depression as increasing.
Table 1 is captioned as 60-day treatment and labels final values as the final visit, whereas surrounding narrative also discusses 90-day observation and 90-day outcomes.
The abstract describes treatment-associated reductions, but the reported values are predominantly within-group changes; no complete between-group effect estimate or confidence interval is provided.

Results locates depression increase between30 and60days; Discussion locates increase after stopping treatment at60days. Reported signed differences−1.0/−0.6 versus wording increase are retained; no direction or time correction inferred.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: The open-label wait-list crossover design and incomplete outcome data may introduce performance and attrition bias.

pooled_events.event: Food-related anaphylactic reaction during washout followed by methylprednisolone treatment
pooled_events.attribution: Not attributed to BLT; severity classification not explicitly reported.

adverse_events.denominator_note: Two withdrawals during BLT across the two randomized sequences. Exact exposed-person denominator not reported; no incidence percentage calculated. Anaphylactic event occurred during washout. No explicit serious-event/death totals.

follow_up.schedule: From randomization: two-week period 1, two-week washout, two-week period 2. Screening occupies approximately one prior week. Post-BLT observation differs by assigned sequence.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: The first-period exploratory analysis showed a 2.75-point improvement with BLT, p = 0.03; the full crossover treatment effect was not significant, p = 0.14.

summary: Randomized two-period crossover trial of bright light therapy and wait list in 36 IOM-defined ME/CFS participants. The full-crossover CFQ coefficient is wait list minus BLT 1.27 (95% CI -0.40 to 2.94; p=.14). Model coefficients estimate median changes. Supplementary exploratory analyses and source inconsistencies are retained separately for synthesis review.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Main report and all 31 supplement pages reviewed. Six clinical outcomes retain 186 sequence/overall descriptive summaries across distinct full-cohort and model-subset tables. Full-crossover median model coefficients are separated from first-period exploratory and baseline association results. Source caption, threshold and CI/p discrepancies remain held.

study_design.design_type_detail: randomized 2x2 crossover trial with BLT and wait-list periods separated by 2-week washout
study_design.randomization_method: An online randomization tool was used.

key_inclusion_criteria: ME/CFS diagnosis according to Institute of Medicine 2015 criteria
Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire score of at least 18 points
key_exclusion_criteria: pAHI at least 15 events per hour

per_arm.n_randomized_quote: A total of 17 patients were randomly assigned to the sequence BLT -washout -wait list

withdrawal_reasons.reason: anaphylactic reaction caused by food and subsequent treatment with methylprednisolone

per_arm.n_randomized_quote: 19 patients were randomly assigned to the sequence wait list -washout -BLT.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: The open-label wait-list crossover design and incomplete outcome data may introduce performance and attrition bias.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: The first-period exploratory analysis showed a 2.75-point improvement with BLT, p = 0.03; the full crossover treatment effect was not significant, p = 0.14.

record.summary: This randomized crossover trial evaluated 2 weeks of 10,000-lux bright light therapy in 36 outpatients with ME/CFS. BLT was not significantly superior to wait list for fatigue in the full crossover analysis, although first-period fatigue improved by 2.75 points (p = 0.03), and Alertness without signal reaction time favored BLT by 69.71 ms (p = 0.04).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm means and SDs for post-treatment outcomes were not provided in the supplied text; several results were reported only as model estimates or in figures/supplementary tables. The supplied Table 1/Table 2 labels appear transposed relative to their contents. Four dropout reasons are listed without explicit arm assignment; adverse-event withdrawals were attributed to BLT based on the stated reasons.

issues.reason: Treatment coefficients are median quantile-regression effects, not independent-group mean differences. Tables 3/4 describe 36/34 overlapping participants by randomized sequence. Descriptive difference formulas and some summary labels are unspecified. Synthesis must preserve pairing and estimand.

Supplement Table 5 caption names Go/No.go although main text and covariate identify first-period CFQ; baseline CFQ CI excludes zero despite p=.18. Main versus supplement CFQ eligibility thresholds differ. Printed source discrepancies retained.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: Randomization, allocation concealment, and handling of missing outcome data were not described in this report.

summary: In female patients meeting CDC criteria for CFS, four weeks of anakinra versus placebo produced a statistically significant difference in hair cortisol change: a decrease with anakinra and an increase with placebo (Cohen’s d = 0.73, p = 0.022). Salivary cortisol changes in CAR, AUCg, and AUCi were not statistically different between groups. At baseline, CFS patients had lower cortisol awakening response and hair cortisol than healthy controls.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper combines baseline CFS-versus-healthy-control comparisons with an anakinra-versus-placebo trial. Table 2 HTML is severely garbled; AUCg, AUCi, and HCC rows were reconstructed from the displayed cell sequence and accompanying text. AUCg and AUCi baseline arm means were not reported in text and are figure-only.

title: Hair and salivary cortisol in a cohort of women with chronic fatigue syndrome
authors: Megan E. Roerink; Sean H.P.P. Roerink; Nadine Skoluda; Marieke E. van der Schaaf; Ad R.M.M. Hermus; Jos W.M. van der Meer; Hans Knoop; Urs M. Nater

study_design.design_type_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 2-period crossover
study_design.randomization_method: Computer-generated randomization sequence prepared by the clinical trial pharmacist.
study_design.setting: Single-center general internal medicine outpatient clinic at a tertiary-care university hospital

source_design_and_timing.design: Randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, crossover study.
source_design_and_timing.site: General internal medicine outpatient clinic at a Belgian tertiary-care university hospital.
source_design_and_timing.treatment_duration: 6 months total; each treatment period lasted 3 months.
source_design_and_timing.sequence: Participants received both placebo and active treatment, in randomized sequence.
source_design_and_timing.washout: No washout period at crossover; authors considered washout unnecessary because each period lasted 3 months.
source_design_and_timing.blinding: Patients and investigators were blinded; active and placebo compounds were indistinguishable in appearance and taste; pharmacist retained computer-generated randomization codes until study end.
source_design_and_timing.eligibility: Adults fulfilling 1994 CDC chronic fatigue syndrome criteria, informed consent, at least four CDC minor criteria, normal screening evaluation.

outcome_definitions.abbreviated_fatigue_questionnaire: Four questions, 7-point Likert scale, total range 4–28; lower score indicates greater fatigue.

source_dose_and_delivery.administration: Investigator dispensed medication at each visit.
source_dose_and_delivery.acth_test: 250 μg ACTH injection at baseline and after each treatment period; cortisol measured at 0, 30, and 60 minutes.
external_doses_discussed: McKenzie et al.: hydrocortisone 13 mg/m² every morning and 3 mg/m² every afternoon.
Cleare et al.: hydrocortisone 5 or 10 mg/day.

summary: One hundred patients were randomized to two sequences;80 completed both three-month treatment periods and75 had complete HADS/SF36 data. All four tables and10 cortisol-defined subgroup comparisons are retained. Shared baselines and paired placebo-minus-treatment effects are distinguished, including lower ACTH-stimulated cortisol on steroids. The flowchart, response definition and one printed confidence interval contain unresolved inconsistencies.

source_limitations: Single published report reviewed across pages 736–741.
No supplementary appendix, protocol, statistical analysis plan, individual participant data, or source datasets were provided.
No complete adverse-event table, treatment-emergent event denominator, or systematic safety analysis was reported.
No exact allocation concealment details beyond pharmacist-held computer-generated codes were provided.
No numerical washout or carryover analysis was reported.
No exact sex count for nonfemale participants was stated beyond 73 females.
No exact denominators were supplied for all dropout percentages because most dropout data were counts only.
The report provides selected subgroup analyses but no prespecified subgroup interaction/model estimates.

summary: Ninety-nine patients received assignment to three IVIG doses or placebo. All17 table rows, pooled time trends, four-group comparisons and harms are retained. Four IVIG recipients received incomplete courses but were reassessed; their doses are unreported. Native POMS energy signs are restored. The paper contains inconsistent low-dose symptom percentages and infusion totals; no pairwise efficacy estimate is reconstructed.

summary: This paper developed and validated the FibroFatigue observer rating scale in 100 women meeting fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome criteria who participated in a 24-week double-blind staphylococcus toxoid vaccine/placebo trial. CPRS-9 scores improved significantly among CGI-C responders, with significant correlations with CGI-C and FIQ changes, while nonresponders showed no significant change. The paper did not report arm-specific treatment efficacy results or adverse-event counts.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The report is primarily a scale-development and validation analysis of a parent vaccine/placebo trial. Per-arm randomized sample sizes and most arm-specific endpoint means are not reported; Table 1 is pooled baseline data, Table 2 is stratified by CGI-C response rather than treatment arm, Table 3 reports vaccine-group changes, and Table 4 reports interrater correlations.

summary: In 60 patients with chronic fatigue syndrome, 13 sessions of cognitive-behavior therapy with graded activity and rest were compared with relaxation. At 6 months, improvement was substantially more frequent after CBT than relaxation (19/27 [70%] vs 5/26 [19%], p<0.001), while physical illness attributions did not change or predict outcome. CBT reduced beliefs favoring exercise avoidance and activity reduction.

summary: This open-label multicentre randomized trial compared individual cognitive behaviour therapy with guided support groups and natural course in adults with chronic fatigue syndrome. CBT was significantly more effective than both control conditions at 14 months for fatigue severity and functional impairment, although complete-case follow-up and per-arm post-treatment descriptive data were incompletely reported in the supplied text.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The supplied text ends during the Results section after Table 1. Follow-up per-arm means, SDs, sample sizes at 14 months, p-values, and most secondary-outcome results are therefore not reported in the supplied text. The summary reports model-based 14-month contrasts for fatigue severity and functional impairment but no exact p-values. The source states 241 complete data at 8 months with 83 CBT, 80 support groups, and 78 natural course.

record.summary: In adults with CFS and severe fatigue and functional impairment, 8 months of cognitive behaviour therapy was compared with guided support groups and natural course. summary: This four-arm randomized PACE trial compared adaptive pacing therapy, cognitive behaviour therapy, and graded exercise therapy, each added to specialist medical care, with specialist medical care alone in 641 adults meeting Oxford chronic fatigue syndrome criteria. The supplied text describes the design and prespecified outcomes but contains no results tables or numerical outcome results, so treatment effects and statistical significance cannot be determined here.

record.summary: In participants with chronic fatigue syndrome, cognitive behaviour therapy and graded exercise therapy generally produced better 52-week secondary outcomes than adaptive pacing therapy or specialist medical care alone. Improvements were statistically significant for work and social adjustment, sleep, depression, and postexertional malaise, while graded exercise therapy improved 6-min walking distance; effects were inconsistent for anxiety, symptom count, and concentration or memory.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Source section contains Tables 5 and 6 only. Table 6 reports baseline and 52-week means (SDs), follow-up questionnaire Ns, and adjusted between-group estimates without confidence intervals. Comparisons reported versus specialist medical care and adaptive pacing therapy; CBT versus GET and other unreported pairwise comparisons were omitted.

record.summary: In the four-arm PACE randomized trial, CBT and GET added to specialist medical care reduced fatigue and improved physical function more than adaptive pacing therapy or specialist medical care alone. Adaptive pacing was no better than specialist medical care alone; the discussion reports moderate effects but does not provide arm-level means, SDs, or exact between-group estimates in this section.

record.summary: In adults with chronic fatigue syndrome, guided graded exercise self-help plus specialist medical care improved work and social adjustment, depression, anxiety, physical activity, and CGI-rated health compared with specialist medical care alone at 12 weeks. Several differences were statistically significant, while general physical symptoms were not significantly improved; serious adverse events and non-serious adverse events were uncommon and similar between groups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This section reports Tables 5–7. Control-group denominators differ across tables: 101 in Tables 5–6 and 102 in Table 7; outcome-specific questionnaire denominators were retained. Table 7 reports adjusted mean differences and CIs rather than adjusted arm means.

eligibility: CFS criteria and written informed consent.

study_design.design_type_detail: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled 2-period crossover trial
study_design.randomization_method: Balanced design in blocks of four; patients were randomly assigned hydrocortisone first or placebo first.
study_design.setting: Outpatient specialist chronic fatigue syndrome clinics in London and Cambridge

source_design_and_timing.design: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial.
source_design_and_timing.treatment_periods: Each treatment lasted 28 days/1 month; patients received consecutive hydrocortisone and placebo periods.
source_design_and_timing.sequence: Randomly assigned hydrocortisone-first or placebo-first using balanced blocks of four.

summary: This two-arm randomized trial compared intelligent-turtle massage with conventional massage in 182 adults with chronic fatigue syndrome. After two treatment courses, intelligent-turtle massage produced greater symptom-improvement scores and a different therapeutic-effect distribution, with statistically significant between-group differences; post-treatment IgA, IgM, and IgG levels were also significantly higher in the intervention group among the 96 participants assessed.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 1 contains scoring criteria but no participant outcome data. Table 2's x̄±s header is garbled but was interpreted as mean±SD. The control-group baseline sex counts sum to 90 despite a reported group size of 91. Immune outcomes were reported for 49 intervention and 47 control participants, with no explanation for the missing participants. The illustrative case reports a single treated 38-year-old man whose score fell from 47 to 6 and whose IgA, IgM, and IgG levels were 3.6, 2.4, and 13.0 mg/ml, respectively; these single-case values were not included as arm-level trial outcomes.

title: Therapeutic effects of oral NADH on the symptoms of patients with chronic fatigue syndrome
authors: Linda M. Forsyth; Harry G. Preuss; Ana L. MacDowell; Leonard Chiazze Jr.; George D. Birkmayer; Joseph A. Bellanti

source_narrative_results.finding: In 26 analyzed subjects, 8/26 (31%) showed at least 10% improvement while receiving NADH versus 2/26 (8%) while receiving placebo; the article reports P<.05 using a difference-between-two-proportions analysis.
source_narrative_results.population: Randomized double-blind crossover analysis population; treatment-period attribution and paired crossover details were not reported.

source_narrative_results.finding: The abstract reports 8/26 (31%) favorable responders to NADH versus 2/26 (8%) to placebo.

Table 5 reports individual symptom scores for all 26 analyzed subjects at weeks 0, 4, 8, and 12. The article does not identify which weeks corresponded to NADH, placebo, or washout for each participant.
Using a self-evaluated questionnaire, 9/26 (35%) subjects correctly identified the treatment period during which they were receiving NADH.

In a longer open-label follow-up, 18/25 (72%) patients reportedly enrolled thus far reported significant improvement in clinical symptomatology and energy levels. This was selected/open-label follow-up evidence, not randomized evidence.
The reported response was characterized by improvement in fatigue, decrease in symptoms, and improvement in quality of life; no separate numerical results were provided for these domains.

No detectable abnormalities were found in serum immunoglobulin concentrations or lymphocyte-subset analyses at baseline or after treatment; further immunologic testing was discontinued after the first patient group. No correlation between immune function, clinical status, or treatment response was established.
No differences in oxidoreductase activity were observed before versus after NADH treatment.

Urinary 5-HIAA concentrations were elevated before treatment in 50% of patients (P<.05); after NADH treatment, these elevated concentrations returned to the normal range. The denominator was not specified.

Blood pressure and hand dynamometry were measured throughout the study, with no significant difference reported. Patients with hypertension 1/26, hypotension 2/26, and normotension did not show a decrease in blood pressure after NADH.

Among the first group of 15, 9/15 (60%) had EBV-EA >1:40. Six of 15 (40%) had HHV-6 titers >1:160 in the table; narrative text states titers >=1:160. One of 26 was anti-HCV positive. Elevated IgE was detected in 2/15 (13%). All subjects tested were HIV-negative and rheumatoid-factor negative. T4 and TSH were within normal limits for all subjects.

In healthy-subject validation work, average mean symptom scores ranged from 0.01 to 0.13 versus 10.9 to 55.8 in CFS patients (P<.001). This was not a randomized treatment comparison in the present study.

source_companion_notes: The article cites a manuscript in preparation on urinary 5-HIAA concentrations as a predictive marker of NADH efficacy in CFS (Forsyth et al., 1998); it was not supplied.
The article cites an open-label follow-up study but provides no companion report or protocol.
No supplementary tables, datasets, statistical analysis plan, or individual randomization/sequence records were supplied.
Potential earlier companion abstract: Bellanti et al. NADH and chronic fatigue syndrome. Ann Allergy Asthma Immunol1998;80:82. Cited by this report; overlap not independently adjudicated.

summary: In this double-blind randomized trial of 100 women meeting fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome criteria, 6 months of subcutaneous Staphypan Berna injections was compared with placebo. Staphylococcus toxoid improved CGI-C response, CPRS-15 symptoms, illness severity, and pain more than placebo, with statistically significant differences for the main outcomes. Symptoms and pain worsened after withdrawal, suggesting that maintenance treatment may be needed.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: A tendency toward reduced clinical response was noted among patients with nickel allergy, especially when also cigarette smokers; nickel allergy and smoking were equally common between groups.

record.summary: This double-blind randomized trial evaluated repeated staphylococcus toxoid injections for six months in women meeting criteria for both fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome. The active-treatment group showed clinically important improvement in CPRS symptoms, particularly fatigue, sleep, memory and concentration, with significant between-group change-from-baseline findings, but deteriorated during the eight-week withdrawal period. Headache was more frequent with active treatment, while overall side-effect ratings were not significantly different.

summary: In this double-blind placebo-controlled trial, women meeting criteria for both fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome received subcutaneous staphylococcus toxoid vaccine or sterile water for 12 weeks. Vaccine treatment significantly improved CPRS fatiguability, CPRS pain, and clinician-rated global improvement versus placebo, while both groups improved on several pain measures; pressure pain thresholds and depression scores were also reported without complete between-group effect estimates.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 1 text is merged and partially garbled; CPRS pain placebo values and some pressure-threshold row labels are difficult to align. The paper reports medians and ranges, not means and SDs. Laboratory abnormalities were reported overall rather than per randomized arm: 2/24 increased plasma homocysteine, 10/12 subnormal CSF vitamin B12, 11/11 high CSF homocysteine, and 2/12 increased CSF methylmalonic acid.

No arm-specific numerical randomized treatment contrasts were reported.
Most outcomes were reported only for the 17 completers, with no intention-to-treat analysis described.

No detailed quality-of-life scores, clinical symptom scores, work-status denominator beyond the 17 completers, or safety outcomes were reported.
No treatment administration route, adherence measurements, or safety-test denominators were reported.
The report is a brief preliminary study and does not provide supplementary outcome data.

summary: In adults meeting Oxford criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome, the PACE trial compared CBT or GET plus specialist medical care with adaptive pacing therapy or specialist medical care alone. Fear avoidance beliefs were the strongest reported mediator of improvements in fatigue and physical function, with larger standardized mediated effects for GET than CBT; GET effects were also mediated by 6-minute walk distance.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The supplied text contains no numerical tables or per-arm means, SDs, or sample sizes. Numeric mediation effects are reported only in the Summary, with effects multiplied by 10; CIs are presented in the same order as effect values. The full Results section and figures/tables are not included.

summary: This long-term follow-up assessed adults with Oxford-criteria chronic fatigue syndrome originally randomized to SMC alone, APT, CBT, or GET. Improvements in fatigue and physical functioning after CBT and GET were maintained, while APT and SMC participants improved during follow-up; long-term outcomes were similar between groups, with interpretation limited by additional non-randomized treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The supplied text includes Table 1 and Table 2 but omits the main long-term outcome tables or figure values. Table 2 reports treatment-data counts of SMC 115, APT 119, CBT 118, and GET 127; 479 participants had treatment data. Table 1 reports participants versus nonparticipants: age 38·6 (12·0) versus 37·5 (11·4), women 366 (76%) versus 129 (81%), white 451 (94%) versus 144 (91%), international criteria met 319 (66%) versus 108 (68%), London criteria met 252 (52%) versus 77 (48%), depressive disorder 152 (32%) versus 61 (38%), any psychiatric disorder 220 (46%) versus 80 (50%), duration 32 (16-66) versus 30 (18-76) months, and BMI 25·3 (4·8) versus 25·9 (5·4).

record.summary: This four-arm PACE trial follow-up assessed CBT, GET, APT, and SMC in adults with chronic fatigue syndrome. Improvements in fatigue and physical functioning after CBT and GET were sustained at a median 134 weeks; adjusted long-term fatigue differences were not significant, while CBT showed better physical functioning than APT (mean difference 6.4, 95% CI 0.4 to 12.4; p=0.035).

summary: This double-blind randomized trial compared oral (-)-OSU6162 with placebo for 2 weeks in adults with myalgic encephalomyelitis. Both groups improved in fatigue and CGI-C during treatment, but overall between-group differences were not statistically significant. OSU6162 showed greater fatigue improvement among participants receiving stable antidepressant therapy, and prolactin increased significantly more with OSU6162.

summary: This two-arm randomized trial compared family-focused CBT with behaviourally oriented psycho-education in 63 adolescents aged 11-18 years with CFS. At 6 months, school attendance was numerically higher with CBT, but the continuous difference was not statistically significant (mean difference 8.5 percentage points, p=0.42), and dichotomized attendance was also not significantly different (OR 0.95, p=0.93).

record.summary: This parallel-group randomized trial compared 13 sessions of family-focused CBT with four sessions of behaviourally oriented psycho-education in adolescents with CFS. At 6 months, CBT did not significantly improve fatigue, physical functioning, social adjustment, SDQ outcomes, or global improvement compared with psycho-education, although treatment satisfaction numerically favored CBT. School attendance showed a significant group-by-time interaction over follow-up.

summary: This reanalysis examined CBT and related psychological interventions in adults and adolescents with chronic fatigue syndrome. Treatments significantly reduced fatigue severity compared with controls in all three trials, but did not significantly increase physical activity, and bootstrap mediation effects were not statistically significant.

The supplied text contains a duplicated n_withdrawn_source key for one arm in the source schema.

summary: This open-label randomized trial tested a 20-week guided self-instruction CBT-based intervention delivered by psychiatric nurses in 123 adults with CDC-defined CFS. At 6 months, fatigue decreased significantly more than with waiting list control, with a reported mean difference of -8.1 and controlled effect size of 0.70; no significant overall differences were reported for physical or social functioning.

record.summary: This parallel-group randomized trial evaluated guided self-instruction delivered by psychiatric nurses versus a waiting list in adults meeting CDC criteria for CFS. Guided self-instruction significantly reduced fatigue severity and increased the proportion with clinically significant fatigue improvement, while effects on physical functioning, social functioning, and psychological distress were not statistically significant in the full sample.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Numeric outcomes from Table 4 were retained in subgroup_analyses rather than duplicated as separate outcome objects. Psychological-distress post-treatment completion was reported as 52 patients across both conditions without arm-specific counts. The paper reports mixed-model results based on all observed data, while table means are completer summaries.

summary: This four-arm PACE trial analysis evaluated CBT, GET, APT, and SMC in 641 adults with chronic fatigue syndrome. At 52 weeks, CBT and GET reduced muscle pain more than SMC or APT, while CBT and GET reduced joint pain more than APT; GET also reduced fibromyalgia prevalence versus SMC. Effects were statistically significant but small.

record.summary: This parallel-group trial compared face-to-face CBT with telephone CBT in adults meeting CDC Fukuda and Oxford criteria for CFS. summary: In adults meeting CDC criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome, stepped care consisting of guided self-instruction followed by CBT when desired was compared with usual CBT after a waiting period. At posttreatment, fatigue, disability, and physical functioning outcomes were similar between groups, with no statistically significant between-group differences; stepped care was reported as noninferior and more therapist-time efficient.

Pragmatic rehabilitation improved several fatigue-related behavioral and cognitive mediators, including catastrophizing and activity limitation, while no between-group differences were found in step-test measures.

summary: This single-center randomized trial tested a 12-week online FATIGUEWALK multicomponent program plus usual care versus usual care alone in 428 adults with CFS/ME. The supplied text reports statistically significant post-treatment improvements in multidimensional fatigue and most secondary outcomes, with Cohen’s d values of 0.25 to 0.73, but does not provide post-treatment arm-level means or SDs.

summary: This pilot trial randomized adults with CFS to 10 sessions of acupuncture or moxibustion every other day and compared them with healthy volunteers. FAI fatigue scores reportedly decreased in all groups, with moxibustion lower than acupuncture after the 10th treatment, while acupuncture produced more immediate HRV changes and moxibustion more long-term changes. Numerical outcome data were presented only in figures, so means, standard deviations, and effect estimates could not be extracted.

summary: This double-blind randomized trial evaluated 8 weeks of low-dose clonidine versus placebo in adolescents with chronic fatigue syndrome. Clonidine was associated with fewer steps, worse sleep quality, poorer quality of life, and reduced orthostatic tolerance among participants homozygous for the COMT val/val high-activity allele; the primary Steps Taken interaction was statistically significant, as were interactions for KSQ and PedsQL.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Both doses appeared to increase leptin versus placebo, but only 10 mg was statistically significant; 5 mg P=0.13 and 10 mg P=0.005.
Responders had a larger hydrocortisone-induced leptin increase than nonresponders.
Leptin correlated positively with BMI in CFS patients (r=0.35, P=0.035) and in all subjects (r=0.26, P=0.04).

summary: In 32 medication-free adults with CFS, 28 days of low-dose oral hydrocortisone increased plasma leptin compared with placebo in the combined-dose analysis (P=0.006). The effect was statistically significant for 10 mg (P=0.005) but not 5 mg (P=0.13), and responders had a larger leptin increase than nonresponders (P=0.047).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Treatment-arm leptin means and SDs were presented only in Figure 1 and are not numerically stated in the text. Table 1 is densely merged and malformed in the supplied text. Arm IDs are used for the randomized hydrocortisone/placebo comparison; baseline CFS-versus-control outcomes reuse these IDs to preserve reported cohort data. No adverse-event data were reported.

summary: Randomized-sequence crossover study of melatonin and bright light in Oxford-criteria CFS: 42 entered and 30 completed. Symptoms were compared before and after each treatment, pooling both sequences. Tables report medians and IQRs for symptoms and means with SEMs for circadian measures. Missing data, unmasked light treatment, period comparisons and source inconsistencies limit causal interpretation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: All seven pages, five tables and Figure 1 reviewed. Extracted 19 clinical outcomes, three circadian measures and three phase correlations. Checked all 76 median/IQR rows and nine mean/SEM rows against native tables. P values concern paired comparisons within each treatment period. Preserved the missing mental-health P value and ambiguous role-physical IQR. Reference 6 (Clin Physiol 1996;16:327–337) describes earlier circadian observations; shared participants are not established. No supplement identified. Linbury Trust funding reported.

summary: This randomized trial evaluated 18 months of cognitive behavioral therapy aided by biofeedback in Egyptian adolescents with chronic fatigue syndrome. Compared with symptomatic care, the intervention significantly reduced fatigue severity and increased school attendance at the end of treatment, although substantial attrition and group switching create a high risk of bias.

record.summary: In Egyptian adolescents with chronic fatigue syndrome, CBT aided by biofeedback was compared with symptomatic treatment over 18 months. End-of-trial self-rated unrefreshing sleep, headache, and myalgia scores favored the intervention with statistically significant p-values of 0.002, 0.03, and 0.005, respectively, while joint pains and tender glands were not significant.

source_design_and_timing.design: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized two-period crossover trial; the same patients received both treatments, so treatment groups were not independent parallel arms.
source_design_and_timing.setting: National Institutes of Health Clinical Center.
source_design_and_timing.eligibility: Adults with debilitating chronic fatigue of no clear cause, CDC chronic-fatigue criteria for at least 1 year, ability to comply, and either EBV diffuse/restricted early-antigen antibody titer ≥1:40 or absent EBNA antibody <1:2.
source_design_and_timing.planned_sample: Initial design called for 24 participants, with replacement of dropouts or adverse-reaction withdrawals.
source_design_and_timing.power_assumption: Sample size stated as sufficient for P<0.05 detection of a difference in proportions improving, with power 0.80, assuming 65% benefit with acyclovir and 20% improvement with placebo.
source_design_and_timing.blinding: Study code remained sealed until all participants completed; treatment could be unblinded for serious adverse responses.
source_design_and_timing.assessments: Admissions at beginning and end of each phase; serial blinded physician examinations. Weekly mailed self-assessments, daily temperature/activity/energy/wellness recordings, daily adverse-effect and treatment-guess recordings during treatment, and Profile of Mood States once per study week for 28 weeks.

source_dose_and_delivery.intravenous: Acyclovir or placebo 500 mg/m², infused over 60 minutes in 150 mL saline every 8 hours for 7 days during hospitalization.
source_dose_and_delivery.oral: Acyclovir 800 mg tablets or placebo four times daily for 30 days after discharge.
source_dose_and_delivery.permitted_concomitant_medications: Vitamins, nonsteroidal and nonnarcotic analgesics, decongestants, antihistamines, oral contraceptives, and antibiotics for documented infections.
source_dose_and_delivery.abstract_wording: Each course consisted of IV placebo or acyclovir 500 mg/m² every 8 hours for 7 days, followed by oral treatment for 30 days; observation periods were 6 weeks before, between, and after treatments.

No other medical diagnosis established
Met Centers for Disease Control chronic fatigue syndrome criteria
Epstein-Barr virus early-antigen titer >=1:40 or absent EBNA antibodies <1:2
Able to comply with the research protocol

source_participant_flow.withdrawal_reason: Reversible renal failure during acyclovir infusion; all 3 cases associated with low back pain, agitation, creatinine elevation, and crystalluria.
source_participant_flow.treatment_sequence: Participants were randomly assigned to acyclovir or placebo for the first treatment and then crossed over to the alternate treatment after washout; sequence groups were reportedly well matched, but sequence counts were not reported.
source_participant_flow.analysis_populations: Clinical improvement denominator was 24 completers; Table 1 and entry-symptom Table 2 describe 27 enrolled participants. Exact denominators for every other analysis are not consistently stated.

source_narrative.text: Twenty-seven adults were enrolled; 3 had reversible renal failure during acyclovir infusions and were withdrawn. Of 24 completers, 21 reported improvement during one treatment phase. Eleven felt better during acyclovir and 10 during placebo. Improvement usually began during the first treatment week and lasted 2–3 weeks after treatment; 4 reported persistence for at least 1 year. Three of those 4 began sustained improvement during placebo; none of the four considered themselves totally normal; they remained more easily fatigued. No clinical, chemical, immunologic, or serologic feature distinguished acyclovir improvers from nonimprovers. Patients whose fatigue began with infectious mononucleosis or a similar illness were not more likely to improve with acyclovir.

reported_results.note: The 11 and 10 responders belong to the same crossover cohort of 24. No independent-arm ratio or joint response table is inferred.

outcomes.name: Epstein-Barr virus viral capsid antigen antibody geometric mean titer
outcomes.synthesis_population: Seropositive adults with chronic fatigue syndrome at study entry

source_narrative.text: Cytomegalovirus antibody geometric mean titers were higher than in age- and sex-matched controls, P=0.05. HSV-1 and HSV-2 titers were not higher than controls, P>0.2 for both. EBV viral-capsid-antigen and early-antigen geometric mean titers in seropositive adults were 1:563 and 1:22, respectively. IgM viral-capsid antibodies were never detected. IgA viral-capsid antibodies at titers ≥1:5 occurred in 63% of patients versus 22% of controls. Four patients had no detectable EBNA antibodies; one other lacked EBNA-1 antibodies alone. Among EBNA-positive patients, 55% had higher EBNA-2 than EBNA-1 titers. EBV antibody levels were remarkably stable; only a minority of later specimens had twofold increases or decreases, and only 1 specimen among those from 4 patients had a fourfold change to a single EBV antigen. Decreases were more common than increases, without correlation with treatment or clinical improvement.

reported_results.note: Pooled baseline/serial serology findings, not acyclovir-arm endpoint evidence. Percentages are retained without inferred event counts or control denominators.

outcomes.name: Other immunologic findings and specimen-level comparisons
outcomes.outcome_concept: Other immunologic findings and specimen-level comparisons
outcomes.synthesis_population: Adults meeting Centers for Disease Control chronic fatigue syndrome criteria

source_narrative.text: Two patients had weakly positive heterophil antibody titers on 3 total occasions. One had low-positive rheumatoid factor (<1:80); 3 had intermittent low-positive antinuclear antibody (<1:80); none met other serologic or major diagnostic criteria for rheumatoid arthritis or lupus. One patient had consistently low IgG, 4.30–5.13 g/L versus normal 6.50–16.00; another had low IgA, 0.31–0.48 g/L versus normal 0.65–4.15; 2 others each had low IgG or IgA on some determinations. Elevated C1q-binding levels occurred in 26/76 patient serum samples versus 3/27 control samples. Elevated Raji-cell-assay immune-complex levels occurred in 10/63 patient samples versus 1/27 controls, with Ti/Ui ratio ≥1.0. Leukocyte 2′,5′-oligoadenylate synthetase levels ranged widely, fluctuated, and were higher in patients than controls, P<0.05. Interferon >4 IU/mL occurred in 10/73 patient samples, range 6–25 IU/mL, versus 2/23 control samples, range 6–25 IU/mL. Interferon content did not correlate with 2′,5′-oligoadenylate synthetase. Suppressor-cell activity was highly variable and had no obvious relation to treatment or clinical status.

outcomes.name: Routine laboratory treatment findings
outcomes.synthesis_population: Adults meeting Centers for Disease Control chronic fatigue syndrome criteria

source_narrative.text: Routine laboratory analyses showed no differences between acyclovir and placebo for white-cell count, red-cell count, platelet count, hematocrit, albumin, alanine aminotransferase, bilirubin, cholesterol, creatinine, glucose, or uric acid. Intravenous acyclovir significantly increased sedimentation rate, P<0.005 by Wilcoxon test. Oral acyclovir increased mean erythrocyte hemoglobin content from 1.94 to 1.97 fmol, P<0.01 for paired differences by t-test, and mean erythrocyte volume from 92.08 to 93.87 fL, P<0.001. Similar erythrocyte-index changes occurred versus pretreatment; values remained within the normal range.

reported_results.analysis: Reported paired/serial laboratory comparisons; no participant-level SD, effect CI or missing count inferred.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: The randomization procedure and allocation concealment were not reported, and three participants withdrew because of acyclovir-induced nephrotoxicity.

source_narrative.major_harm: Three patients developed reversible renal failure during acyclovir infusions and were withdrawn. Creatinine rose as high as 725 μmol/L (8.2 mg/dL); crystalluria occurred despite hydration attempts.
source_narrative.treatment_related_summary: More gastrointestinal symptoms occurred with acyclovir, P=0.03; headaches and dizziness were also reported more often in drug recipients.
source_narrative.adverse_experience_table: All numerical cells are in Table 5. Counts are symptom occurrences counted once per patient per IV or oral course, not necessarily unique participants across phases or routes.
source_narrative.routine_laboratory_harms: No treatment differences for the listed routine laboratory variables; IV acyclovir increased sedimentation rate and oral acyclovir produced small erythrocyte-index increases as specified in narrative_results.

adverse_events.counting_rule: Each symptom is counted only once for each patient during a course of intravenous or oral treatment.

source_schedule.caption: Design of the Placebo (PLC)-Controlled Acyclovir (ACV) Trial.
source_schedule.description: Five sequential phases: 6-week pretreatment observation, 37-day treatment phase, 6-week washout, 37-day alternate-treatment phase, and 6-week post-treatment observation. Each treatment phase consisted of 7 days of inpatient IV medication followed by 30 days of oral medication. Patients were randomly assigned to acyclovir then placebo or placebo then acyclovir. Open boxes indicate NIH Clinical Center admissions; admissions occurred at the beginning and end of each phase, six admissions total.
plot_only_fields: Individual timeline graphics and exact plotted spacing are not used to infer additional values.

follow_up.duration_note: The report describes weekly POMS across 28 study weeks, two 37-day treatment periods, and six-week observation periods before, between and after treatments; no randomization-relative endpoint week is inferred.

summary: This crossover trial enrolled 27 adults; 24 completed both treatment conditions. Eleven felt better with acyclovir and ten with placebo. Three participants withdrew with reversible renal failure during acyclovir infusions. The report did not establish clinical benefit. Paired mood differences, selected improvement-phase comparisons, all five tables and specimen-level findings are retained separately.

summary: This letter reports diary-based predictors from a three-arm randomized self-management trial in people with severe chronic fatigue syndrome. In the high-tech intervention, 10/45 participants improved clinically significantly in fatigue at 12 months versus 4/48 in the no-treatment control; depression symptoms were also significantly lower at follow-up (p = .02).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The report is a brief secondary-analysis letter and does not provide arm-level means or SDs. The third study arm is not identified. Omitted quantitative outcomes due to the requested limit: reduction in feeling pressured (r = -.40; p = .08), diary-rated non-walking exercise (M = 5.73 (2.76)), walking (M = 4.50 (3.04)), relaxation (M = 3.54 (2.19)), and lower-rated support from others, coping ideas, pleasant activities, sleep techniques, and pacing (M = 2.0 -2.9).

summary: This three-arm randomized trial evaluated a 12-week home-based fatigue self-management program in severely ill adults with chronic fatigue syndrome, comparing web diaries and actigraphs or paper diaries and pedometers with usual care. The paper reports lower fatigue at 3 months for the paper-diary intervention versus usual care (p = .03), but no significant fatigue benefit at 12 months; physical functioning did not differ significantly between groups at baseline or 3 months.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 reports SE and 95% CI rather than SD; the SF-36 UC baseline CI appears internally inconsistent with its mean and SE. Per-arm randomized sample sizes and allocation procedures were not reported. Table 3 contains 217 qualitative attribution responses across 20 themes; these counts are not encoded as clinical outcome arm results.

record.summary: A 10-week videoconference cognitive behavioral stress management intervention was compared with a time-matched health-information control in adults with Fukuda-criteria CFS. Among patients with severe baseline PEM, V-CBSM significantly improved symptom frequency, symptom intensity, fatigue interference, and fatigue intensity; perceived stress showed a medium but nonsignificant effect. V-CBSM also reduced the odds of highPEM classification at follow-up, with a trend toward significance.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: The report combined randomized groups for analysis and excluded four delayed-group dropouts, preventing a clear randomized between-group treatment estimate.

summary: This randomized study evaluated a community-based, goal-setting rehabilitation program for adults meeting CDC chronic fatigue syndrome criteria. Goal attainment was significantly associated with quality-of-life improvement after adjustment for fatigue severity, symptom severity, and psychiatric comorbidity (B = 0.234, p < .05), although the randomized groups were combined and no direct between-arm treatment effect was reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The report describes randomization to initial and delayed groups but analyzes participants who received the program in combination. Table 2 reports pooled goal counts rather than arm-specific participant outcomes. The paper contains no per-arm means, SDs, or endpoint quality-of-life values.

summary: This small open-label randomized trial evaluated subcutaneous interferon-alpha-2b three times weekly for 12 weeks in adults with chronic fatigue syndrome. Among 20 participants, 3 completely recovered and 2 improved, with improvement first evident 1-3 months after treatment; no randomized arm-specific comparative effect estimate was reported. Response was significantly associated with detectable coxsackievirus B IgM antibody (chi-square 7.2, P < .01).

source_narrative.text: CGI correlated with improvement in general, physical, and mental fatigue in all groups (r ≥ 0.362, p < .05). CGI correlated with attention concentration in ALC (r = 0.476, p = .010) and ALC + PLC (r = 0.489, p = .006), but not PLC. CGI did not correlate with pain.

reported_results.note: Associations among changes, not causal between-treatment effects.

outcomes.name: Carnitine changes and response correlations
outcomes.synthesis_population: Adults with CFS meeting CDC criteria

source_narrative.text: Plasma L-carnitine increased significantly in all groups, somewhat less in responders. Carnitine esters increased in all groups but remained low relative to L-carnitine. In ALC, the L-carnitine change was inversely related to clinical improvement and related to general and mental fatigue improvement; these relationships were not found in PLC or ALC + PLC. Plasma ALC and PLC were not related to clinical outcome. Change in plasma carnitine was not related to attention-concentration or pain change. No sex difference in carnitine-level increase was reported.

reported_results.note: Exact coefficients not supplied for several associations; preserve reported direction/significance only.

outcomes.name: Separate preliminary carnitine studies
outcomes.synthesis_population: Adults with CFS meeting CDC criteria

source_narrative.text: Prior reports cited: prevalence estimates 1‰–4‰; preliminary open-label L-carnitine study, 150 patients, 1 g bid, 104/150 (69%) markedly improved after 6 months; preliminary randomized double-blind study, n = 18, with 6 low-dose ALC 1 g/d + LC 1 g/d, 6 high-dose twice that dose, and 6 placebo; marked improvement after 6 months in 4 low-dose, 0 high-dose, and 1 placebo participant. These were unpublished or external studies, not randomized evidence from the present trial.

reported_results.note: 150-person open study and18-person pilot are separate cohorts; not counted as additional randomized reports here.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: The open-label design and subjective primary CGI outcome create substantial risk of performance and measurement bias.

source_narrative.other_discontinuations: 8 stopped because they experienced no treatment effect: ALC 4, PLC 1, ALC + PLC 3. Two stopped for reasons unrelated to treatment.
source_narrative.other_adverse_effects: Discussion mentions trimethylamine formation or diarrhea in a few patients in other studies, not as quantified harms in this trial.
source_narrative.safety_tests: No separate safety-test denominator or systematic adverse-event table was reported.

summary: This90-person open randomized carnitine study analyzed29/30/30 participants using nominalITT with carried-forward values. All eight table sections,18 within-arm Friedman tests and three response-stratified carnitine analytes are retained. Flow, response percentages and subgroup counts contain source conflicts. Eight side-effect discontinuations are reported; no placebo-controlled treatment effect is established.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: All seven native pages, eight table sections and flowchart reviewed. Recovered missing ester outcomes, significance superscripts, all18 Friedman statistics, correlations and prior pilot cohorts. Corrected analysisN and removed unreported death zeros; retained source count conflicts and rounded P values.

Friedman tests are within-arm longitudinal tests; response-defined biochemical strata are post-randomization groups. No direct treatment effect is reported. Rounded P0.000, overlapping CGI category footnote and conflicting response counts remain explicit; synthesis pending.

source_figures.caption: Trial profile
source_figures.description: CONSORT-like flow diagram: 114 assessed for eligibility; 12 excluded, all for refusal to participate; 90 randomized, allocated 30 each to ALC, PLC, and ALC + PLC. ALC: 29 received allocated intervention and 1 did not; PLC: 30 received allocated intervention; ALC + PLC: 30 received allocated intervention. Lost to follow-up: 0 in all groups. Discontinued intervention: ALC 8, PLC 4, ALC + PLC 6. Side effects: ALC 3, PLC 2, ALC + PLC 3; no-effect discontinuations: ALC 5, PLC 2, ALC + PLC 3. Analyzed: ALC 29, PLC 30, ALC + PLC 30. Excluded from analysis: ALC 1; PLC 0; ALC + PLC 0. ALC analysis exclusion was refusal of intervention after randomization.

source_limitations: Open-label design without placebo or blinded comparator.
Exploratory sample-size calculation was based on preliminary studies and not powered for ALC-versus-PLC differences.
Primary CGI was subjective and patient-rated.
No formal adjusted between-group treatment contrasts were reported.
No exact denominators were supplied for some narrative percentages beyond the 30-per-group allocation.
No safety-test denominators or comprehensive adverse-event table.
Correlations described as 'not shown' lack numerical estimates.
Figure coordinates beyond printed flow counts are unavailable and were not inferred.
The article itself states that conclusive evidence requires a double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial.
source_contradictions: Figure1 gives114 screened,12excluded and90allocated, leaving12unaccounted. Eligibility count not established.
Narrative lack-of-effect discontinuations4/1/3 plus2unrelated versus figure5/2/3; figure total discontinuations8/4/6. No reassignment inferred.
Table2a PLC24week counts16+10+1=27, percentages63/34/3; figure analysisN30. Retain all values. Table5PLC responders19 versus Table2a16.

Combined CGI follow-up worse12(40%) in table versus37% in narrative/abstract; narrative says three retained improvement but discussion says all improved patients deteriorated. Table5 responders10 versus Table2a11.
CGI no-change footnote-1≤CGI≤+2 overlaps improved≥2; prose calls scale five-point but spans-3to+3.
Narrative78%female versus69/90 in Table1; preserve source counts without replacing one with the other.
Printed P0.000 is rounded, not exact zero.

issues.reason: 114 screened minus12excluded does not yield90randomized. Figure29/30/30 analyzed; narrative/flow reasons and CGI counts/percentages conflict. Exact table-specific Ns unreported; no denominator inferred.

Friedman tests are within-arm longitudinal tests; response-defined biochemical strata are post-randomization groups. No direct treatment effect is reported. Rounded P0.000, overlapping CGI category footnote and conflicting response counts remain explicit; synthesis pending.

_scientific_validation.note: Numerical checks and quote matches do not establish correct table-column attribution.

_source_adjudication.method: Agent native-PDF verification and reconciliation of Codex CLI gpt-5.6-luna medium extraction; not human review
corrections: Corrected eight table-section count and figure analysisN29/30/30.
Retained all18 Friedman chi-square/P results outside generic between-group effects.
Recovered both missing carnitine esters, three between-responder and ten within-subgroup significance markers.
Preserved every CGI count/percentage and timing context without contradictory denominator inference.
Recovered associations, follow-up narrative and separate150-person/18-person preliminary cohorts; removed unknown death zeros.

completion.limitations: All supplied pages, tables, figure annotations and own-study numerical narrative reviewed. Exact graph-only coordinates remain unavailable; source inconsistencies and missing analysis denominators remain explicit. No declared missing supplement identified.

release_limitations.reason: Source data have been reviewed. Documented source limitations and synthesis decisions still prevent numerical conclusions.

study_design.design_type_detail: parallel-group, three-arm randomized controlled trial
study_design.randomization_method: Computer-generated randomization schedule with randomly varying blocks of 6 or 9; assignment emailed to nurse interventionists after baseline assessments.

key_exclusion_criteria: fatigue clearly attributable to identifiable medical conditions

summary: Three-arm randomized trial of nurse-conducted fatigue self-management, symptom-monitoring support and usual care in 111 primary-care participants with CFS or unexplained chronic fatigue. It reports fatigue impact, physical function, depression, anxiety and clinical response at follow-up, using multiple-imputation ITT and separate per-protocol analyses. Final reported arm completion counts were 19, 22 and 18; several source reporting conflicts remain documented.

record.summary: This three-arm randomized trial tested a brief fatigue self-management intervention in primary-care adults with medically unexplained chronic fatigue or CFS. At 12 months, fatigue impact improved more with fatigue self-management than with attention control or usual care, with moderate ITT effects and large per-protocol effects; no significant benefits were found for physical functioning, anxiety, or depression.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Source section includes Table 1 and narrative results but not Table 3; arm-level follow-up means and SDs for FSS, SF-36PF, BAI, and BDI are therefore not reported here. Table 1 additionally reports illness duration, marital status, ethnicity, and employment: illness duration FSM 11.67 (9.11), AC 8.93 (7.45), UC 9.81 (8.37); single/divorced/separated 17 (45.9%), 10 (26.3%), 12 (33.4%); living with partner 14 (37.8%), 25 (65.8%), 19 (52.8%); European 30 (81.1%), 28 (73.7%), 26 (72.2%); Latino 1 (2.7%), 2 (5.3%), 5 (13.9%); Black 1 (2.7%), 2 (5.3%), 1 (2.8%); working full time 16 (43.2%), 21 (55.3%), 20 (55.6%); unemployed 7 (18.9%), 1 (2.6%), 4 (11.1%).

summary: This double-blind randomized trial evaluated intranasal mechanical stimulation in 31 patients with moderate to severe ME meeting Canadian consensus criteria. Active INMEST produced approximately a 30% reduction in overall symptom scores after 8 weeks, significantly greater than placebo followed by active treatment (p=0.00003), while no significant effect was observed for the primary fatigue severity scale outcome.

record.summary: In this open-label randomized crossover trial of adolescents and young adults with QFS, ME/CFS, PCC, or JIA, tailored PROfeel lifestyle advice was compared with generic dietary advice. Fatigue, self-efficacy, and physical and emotional quality of life improved over time, but the two interventions did not differ significantly in improvement. Diet quality did not improve on average, despite moderate adherence ratings.

record.summary: In this open-label randomized crossover trial of adolescents and young adults with QFS, ME/CFS, PCC, or JIA, tailored PROfeel lifestyle advice was compared with generic dietary advice. Fatigue, self-efficacy, and physical and emotional quality of life improved over time, but the two interventions did not differ significantly in improvement. Diet quality did not improve on average, despite moderate adherence ratings.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Numeric endpoint values after intervention were primarily figure-only or unavailable by arm; Table 2 reports adjusted overall time changes rather than per-arm means. The supplied section includes baseline Table 1 values, adjusted Table 2 changes, adherence/feasibility means, diet-quality changes, and subgroup percentages.

source_narrative_results.result: Baseline: the tailored PROfeel lifestyle-advice-first group tended to be older, had higher self-efficacy levels, and had fewer sleep/wake problems.
Fatigue severity improved over time: F(2,89)=8.36, p<.001.
Self-efficacy improved over time: F(2,87)=4.38, p=.015.
Physical functioning QoL improved with clinical relevance: F(2,124)=4.60, p=.012.
Emotional functioning QoL improved with clinical relevance: F(2,131)=6.21, p=.003.
Social functioning QoL did not improve significantly: p=.575.
Work/school functioning QoL did not improve significantly: p=.106.
Marginal R2 was highest for emotional functioning: R2=.540; fatigue severity followed: R2=.314.
No significant differences between interventions in level of improvement: all p>.999.
No statistical relevance of intervention order: p_range=.277 to .831.
Clinically relevant fatigue improvement occurred in 20/46 trial completers (43.48%) and 5/11 dropouts (45.46%), thus 43.86% in total.
Fatigue deteriorated in 3 participants (6.52%).
Feasibility ratings, on a 1-low to 10-high scale: PROfeel lifestyle advice 6.4 (SD=1.96); generic dietary advice 6.5 (SD=1.86).
Self-rated adherence: PROfeel lifestyle advice 7.7 (SD=1.74); generic dietary advice 7.63 (SD=1.59).
Overall diet quality did not improve on average: ΔM=-10.30, SD=20.84.
Whole-wheat products: ΔM=-1.49, SD=3.41.
Processed meats: ΔM=-1.36, SD=3.86.
Unhealthy choices, such as high-sugar snacks: ΔM=-1.04, SD=3.91.
Diet quality decreased in 30 participants: ΔM=-19.36, SD=18.48; was stable in 2; and improved in 14: ΔM=9.79, SD=7.50.
Feasibility, adherence, and overall diet-quality change were not associated with change in fatigue severity, self-efficacy, or QoL at T2 and T4: p_range=.052–.943.
The randomized crossover trial lasted 32 weeks and included AYA with QFS, ME/CFS, PCC, or JIA.
There was a four-month period between T2 and T4, consisting of a four-week washout followed by twelve weeks of self-management.
Average disease duration was 4.41 years.
Figure 3 caption: clinically relevant fatigue improvement was defined as a decrease of ≥6 points on the CIS-8 total score compared with baseline.
Figure 3 caption: no significant frequency differences across subgroups; Kruskal-Wallis H=4.34, p=.227.

study_identity_evidence.evidence: Companion methods explicitly cite Vroegindeweij 2023 as the lifestyle/dietary crossover trial; reference DOI, title and authors match recovered parent PDF. Both describe the same site, interventions and mixed ME/CFS/QFS/PCC/JIA cohort.
study_identity_evidence.limitations: Parent enrollment 60 versus 59 companion patients; healthy controls are additional observational participants. Link reports without assuming identical analysis denominators or counting recruitment twice.

source_narrative.text: Among 25 randomized to LSLY, 7 did not commence because it was too difficult, 3 stopped within 4 weeks, and 9 included foods to avoid on several occasions. Six (24%) were fully compliant for 24 weeks; a further 9 had some dietary breaches, so 15 (60%) attempted to or maintained the diet throughout. Among 27 allocated HE, 9 did not fully adhere: 1 followed an alternative nutritionist and omitted several food groups, 1 became too unwell to continue, and 7 were lost to follow-up. Eighteen (67%) were fully compliant for 24 weeks.

reported_results.definition: Inclusion of food to avoid on more than three occasions during the trial.
reported_results.note: These are adherence outcomes. Nonadherence categories, medication use and losses can overlap and must not be summed.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: The open-label design, self-reported outcomes, substantial attrition and differential adherence create important risk of bias.

reported_adverse_events_or_treatment_dis: 1 HE participant became too unwell to continue the trial.
5 participants received antibiotic therapy during the trial: 3 HE and 2 LSLY.
6 participants were prescribed nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents: 3 HE and 3 LSLY.
2 participants received HRT: 1 HE and 1 LSLY.
source_narrative.other: No systematic adverse-event table or complete harms ascertainment is reported. No inference of zero harms is made.

summary: The 52-person dietary trial reported no significant advantage of low sugar/low yeast over healthy eating for fatigue, quality of life or mood at 24 weeks. Full adherence was 6/25 versus 18/27. All four tables are retained. The report states ITT but presents 39 comparative-analysis participants; overlap between medication use and losses is unclear.

summary: This 63-person randomized trial reported symptom improvement with essential fatty acids over three months. All three tables are retained. The month-one placebo count/percentage row is inconsistent, and biomarker follow-up includes only 19 active and 13 placebo paired samples. The report states no adverse effects and no cures; synthesis remains pending.

summary: Fifty patients were randomized to Efamol Marine or sunflower oil;38 completed three months. All26 numerical table rows and three narrative lipid results are retained. source_limitations: No figures were included.
No individual participant data, allocation concealment details beyond sealed pharmacy-held codes, adherence data, or protocol deviations were reported.
No exact denominators for the Table 2 percentages were provided.
No adverse-event counts or safety-test results were provided.
No confidence intervals, effect sizes, regression coefficients, or detailed model outputs were provided.
The case-control biomarker sample included only the first 25 patients and 25 matched controls, not necessarily the full randomized cohort.
The article does not clearly state whether treatment analyses were intention-to-treat, per-protocol, or based on available cases.
The report is limited to printed pages 112-116.

source_contradictions.details: Narrative calls comparator control within the treatment-results paragraph; no matching table or dispersion is supplied. Preserve wording; no guessed variance or external-control allocation.

sample_size: Fisher exact test for equal numbers; planned power 0.90 and significance level 0.05.
Based on external Behan rates of 85% versus 17%, calculated requirement was 11.85 per group.
Textbook minimum total for a two-sample t-test was 49.
clinical_outcomes: Mann-Whitney U-test compared physical symptom and Beck scores between groups at baseline, 1, 2, and 3 months.
End-of-study change in symptom scores was assessed with the same test.
Patient-reported treatment response was analyzed with chi-squared test.
biomarkers: Independent t-tests compared patients with age- and sex-matched controls.
Within the patient group, changes and absolute symptom scores were correlated with changes and absolute blood-lipid levels using linear stepwise multiple regression.
source_statistical_methods.missing_model_outputs: No regression coefficients, confidence intervals, sample sizes, or detailed predictor results reported.

study_design.design_type_detail: parallel-group, two-arm pragmatic multicentre randomized controlled trial

arms.label: Multidisciplinary rehabilitation treatment

source_delivery.limitation: Different contact intensity across arms; this trial does not isolate individual treatment components.
table1_components: Combination of mindfulness-based CBT, gradual reactivation, body awareness therapy, pacing, social reintegration
Focus on healthy bodily symptoms and increasing body awareness
First time-contingent increase in activity, later increase in activity with feedback of healthy bodily symptoms (during treatment sessions and home exercises)
Protocol tailored to the individual patient
Focus of treatment: components that are thought to be modifiable and have a strong correlation with the precipitation, predisposition and perpetuation of CFS
Direct feedback during activity (in treatment session) and after home exercises (in following treatment session)
Therapists: consultant in rehabilitation medicine, physical therapist, occupational therapist, psychologist or cognitive behavioural therapist, social worker

arms.label: Cognitive behavioural therapy
arms.frequency: weekly for 6 weeks, then biweekly for 20 weeks

source_delivery.limitation: Different contact intensity across arms; this trial does not isolate individual treatment components.
table1_components: Ignore bodily symptoms of fatigue and pain
Protocol tailored to relatively active and passive patient
Focus of treatment: components that are thought to have a strong correlation with the perpetuation of CFS.
Feedback after home exercises in following therapy session
Therapist: psychologist or cognitive behavioural therapist

record.summary: In adults meeting CDC-94 criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome, multidisciplinary rehabilitation treatment was compared with cognitive behavioural therapy in a two-arm randomized trial. MRT produced significantly lower fatigue severity than CBT at 52 weeks, but not at 26 weeks, while quality-of-life differences were not statistically significant. MRT also improved self-efficacy, personal goals, and satisfaction with treatment.

summary: This open-label randomized trial evaluated the Lightning Process added to specialist medical care in 100 adolescents aged 12-18 years with paediatric CFS/ME. Compared with specialist medical care alone, the intervention significantly improved SF-36 physical function at 6 months and also improved fatigue, anxiety, depression, school attendance, and 12-month QALYs, although arm-level follow-up means and SDs were not provided in the supplied text.

record.summary: In adults meeting Oxford criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome without current psychiatric disorder or symptomatic insomnia, 12 weeks of graded aerobic exercise was compared with flexibility and relaxation therapy. Exercise produced significantly greater clinically important improvement by intention-to-treat analysis (17/33 versus 9/33; P=0.04), along with better fatigue, physical function, aerobic capacity, and submaximal exercise responses. Benefits were reported as maintained at three months and one year, although the open-label design and self-rated outcomes create some risk of bias.

title: Randomised controlled trial of patient education to encourage graded exercise in chronic fatigue syndrome
