source_narrative_results.population: Intention-to-treat; 148 randomized participants, with last values carried forward for dropouts
source_narrative_results.result: 79 (69%) of patients in the three intervention groups achieved a satisfactory SF-36 physical-functioning outcome versus 2 (6%) controls receiving standardized medical care; P < 0.0001.
source_narrative_results.definition: SF36 physical functioning≥25 or increase≥10 from baseline at12months; range10–30. Both inequality signs verified in native abstract/Methods.

source_narrative_results.result: At one year, physical-functioning outcomes differed across groups: F(3,142)=24.15, P <0.001. Each intervention group had a higher mean score than control, P <0.001 for each comparison; no difference was observed among intervention groups.

At one-year follow-up, fatigue improvement differed across groups: F(3,142)=24.99, P <0.001. Each intervention group improved more than control, P <0.001 for each comparison; no differences were observed among intervention groups.

Patients meeting the improvement criterion: control 2/34; minimum intervention 26/37; telephone intervention 27/39; maximum intervention 26/38. chi-square=42.54, df=3, P <0.001. Reported NNTs were 1.55, 1.58, and 1.60 respectively for minimum, telephone, and maximum intervention versus control.
Among patients who completed educational intervention, 84% (80/95) reported being 'very much better' or 'much better', versus 12% (4/32) of control patients.

source_narrative_results.population: 77 intervention-group patients completed illness-belief questionnaires; two questionnaires were incomplete
results: Belief that illness was caused by a persistent virus: 81% (61/75) before treatment and 23% (17/75) at one year.
Belief that illness was due to a missed physical illness: 67% (50/75) at baseline and 13% (10/75) at one year.
Belief that illness was related to physical deconditioning: 15% (11/75) at baseline and 81% (61/75) after treatment.
Avoidance of physical activity: 82% (63/77) before treatment and 6% (5/77) after treatment.
Explanations convinced 94% (72/77) to carry out graded activity.
source_narrative_results.timing_note: Questionnaires administered at one year; pretreatment beliefs recalled retrospectively. These are not independently observed prospective baseline-to-follow-up measurements.

source_narrative_results.result: Interventions improved fatigue, physical functioning, mood, sleep, and disability scores; gains were reported as maintained at one-year follow-up. The control-group improvement was described as similar to that observed elsewhere.

Of patients who completed treatment, 81% met the improvement criterion. The intention-to-treat analysis stated that 32% of patients still complained of fatigue at one year despite substantial improvement in physical functioning; the denominator for this percentage was not specified.

No significant differences were found among minimum, telephone, and maximum intervention groups. The authors stated there was no evidence that additional face-to-face or telephone contacts produced further improvement, while noting that longer-term follow-up might reveal differences.

The authors compared their completion-only 84% better/much-better proportion with 60-74% in other cited trials and cited a review reporting NNT=2 for specialist cognitive behavioural therapy. These are external references, not additional randomized outcomes from this study.

source_companion_notes: A more detailed intervention account adapted for non-ambulatory patients was cited: Powell P, Edwards R, Bentall R. Behavioural and Cognitive Psychotherapy 1999;27:249-260.
No supplementary appendix, protocol, statistical analysis plan, registry record, or companion safety report was included in the reviewed five-page source.

record.summary: In adolescents meeting US CDC criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome, a five-month course of individualized cognitive behaviour therapy was compared with a waiting list. Therapy significantly improved fatigue severity, physical functioning, and school attendance, and increased clinically significant improvement and self-rated recovery. Several additional symptoms also improved, although not all symptom outcomes were statistically significant.

record.summary: Cognitive behavioural therapy was evaluated in adults and adolescents with chronic fatigue syndrome using self-reported cognitive impairment questionnaires and neuropsychological tests. CBT significantly reduced reported cognitive impairment compared with control conditions, with reported Cohen d values of 1.3 and 0.6 in adults and 0.6 and 0.4 in adolescents, while reaction-time and SDMT performance did not significantly improve.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The report combines data from two separate randomized trials and does not provide raw per-arm SDs or endpoint means; Table 1 reports estimated change scores with 95% CIs. Adult questionnaire sample sizes are not explicitly provided, while neuropsychological subset sizes are reported as 78 CBT, 76 natural course, and 79 support group. SDMT data were available for 174 patients, but per-arm counts were not stated. Treatment duration was not reported.

outcomes.name: Patient evaluation and participation
outcomes.synthesis_population: Women with chronic fatigue syndrome diagnosed according to CDC criteria

source_narrative.result: Group 1 had a higher frequency of participation throughout. Sessions focused largely on illness and medical aspects, symptom discussion, alternative treatments, concentration problems, fear of brain damage, accepting changed identity, high ambitions, recognizing limits, asking for and receiving help, and setting limits to demands. The group did not become process-oriented because participants did not refer to previous-session discussions.

Participants valued insight into other sufferers' situations, feeling understood, closeness, and gained insight. They were dissatisfied that sessions felt like a 'nice get-together' and wanted a more active psychologist, more sessions, preferably twice as many over an extended period, smaller groups, session themes, and more active psychologist participation.

The study did not provide a conclusive answer regarding group-therapy effectiveness. The authors suggested that patients may need longer continuous group therapy, smaller groups, more active leadership, individual support, and help formulating specific goals. They recommended, if group therapy is used, a minimum duration of 1 year in small groups.
More than half felt the sessions improved psychological well-being through adjusted ambitions and coping; exact count/denominator unreported.

reported_results.participation: Group1 participated more frequently and was more satisfied;no attendance counts supplied
reported_results.note: Qualitative process and participant appraisal,not randomized responder data. Suggested minimum one-year therapy was a recommendation,not this study duration.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: The open-label design, small sample, incomplete follow-up in the waiting-list group, and unclear allocation concealment limit confidence in the findings.

source_narrative.adverse_events: No adverse-event outcomes, harms, withdrawals for adverse events, or safety assessments were reported.
source_narrative.clinical_observations: Some participants had traumatic family experiences, depression, relationship problems, or sex problems mentioned during discussions; these were contextual discussion topics, not reported treatment-emergent adverse events.

follow_up.schedule_note: Group1 before/after immediate therapy;group2 before/after5-month wait and after delayed therapy. Post-therapy visits are not the same time since randomization.

summary: Fourteen women were randomized7/7 to immediate or delayed group therapy. All four quality-of-life table rows and10 mean/SD pairs are retained,with7/6 post-therapy observations. Baseline SOC is pooled across all14. Fatigue was not statistically analyzed because of response ambiguity; patient evaluations are qualitative. No conclusive controlled efficacy estimate or harms accounting is available.

Baseline social-support scores differed by sex and age, and cross-sectional comparisons showed differences in specific support subscales, but no significant group difference in total supporting interactions.

record.summary: This 2x2 factorial randomized trial evaluated distant healing in 409 adults with CFS, comparing immediate versus deferred healing with and without participants' knowledge. Distant healing was not statistically significant for MHCS or PHCS; adjusted PHCS difference was 1.11 points, 95% CI -0.26 to 2.47, p=0.111, while knowledge of treatment status was associated with a small PHCS difference.

study_design.design_type_detail: Open-label alternate-assignment two-period treatment study; no randomized allocation or placebo control

arms.label: Amantadine
arms.dose: 100 mg once daily for 1 month, then 100 mg twice daily if tolerated

source_design_and_timing.report: Plioplys AV, Plioplys S. Amantadine and L-Carnitine Treatment of Chronic Fatigue Syndrome. Neuropsychobiology. 1997;35:16-23. DOI: 10.1159/000119325.
source_design_and_timing.design: Open-label, two-period crossover treatment program; alternate patients were assigned to treatment sequence. The paper does not describe randomization.
source_design_and_timing.periods: First medication for 2 months, 2-week washout, alternate medication for an additional 2 months.
source_design_and_timing.assessment_timing: Before, during, and after each treatment; every 2 weeks during each 2-month treatment period.
source_design_and_timing.comparators: Within-person sequential exposure to amantadine and L-carnitine; no placebo or untreated concurrent control.
source_design_and_timing.washout_and_carryover: A 2-week washout was specified. No formal carryover analysis was reported.
source_design_and_timing.analysis_populations: 30 enrolled; 28 retained after two noncompliance/follow-up exclusions. Amantadine completers: n = 15 at 8 weeks; 4-week tolerant group n = 20. L-carnitine 4-week population: N = 28; 8-week population: N = 27.

source_dose_and_delivery.amantadine: 100 mg once each morning for 1 month; if tolerated, increased after 1 month to 100 mg twice daily, morning and noon.
source_dose_and_delivery.delivery: Medicines provided free of charge; clinical visits and evaluations also free.
source_dose_and_delivery.discontinuation_rules: Medication stopped if adverse effect made continuation impossible or inadvisable; alternate medication started after a 2-week washout. Program discontinued for noncompliance, pregnancy, or intercurrent illness postponing treatment for more than 2 months.

study_design.allocation_method: Alternate patients assigned to L-carnitine or amantadine first

Met Australian and British definitions of chronic fatigue syndrome

key_exclusion_criteria: Intercurrent illness postponing treatment for more than 2 months

source_baseline.concomitant_medicines: Only as-needed nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicines were used; all 28 complied with restrictions on interfering medicines.

outcomes.name: Treatment-sequence comparisons
outcomes.synthesis_population: Adults meeting CDC criteria for CFS

results: After exclusions, 14 patients started with L-carnitine and 14 with amantadine.
No significant baseline differences were found between first-treatment groups for age, sex, onset mode, illness duration, or free, acyl, and total carnitine.
The only significant baseline psychometric difference was PSDI: L-carnitine-first 1.86±0.31 versus amantadine-first 1.68±0.41; p = 0.005.

At the start of L-carnitine, first-versus-second sequence differences were: SCL-90-R DI 1.31±0.62 versus 0.80±0.54; p = 0.028; GSI 0.964±0.395 versus 0.614±0.400; p = 0.028; PSTI 45.72±13.19 versus 29.29±18.11; p = 0.011.

reported_results.sequence_comparison: There was no significant difference at 4 or 8 weeks between the 14 L-carnitine-first and 14 L-carnitine-second patients on any psychometric outcome.
reported_results.note: Nonrandom assignment; sequence and baseline associations, not randomized treatment effects.

record.summary: This pooled reanalysis examined whether CBT caused symptom deterioration in adults and adolescents with CFS compared with care as usual, guided support, or waiting-list controls. Clinically significant deterioration was not more frequent with CBT; it was significantly less frequent for self-rated change, daily observed fatigue, and SIP impairment, while other comparisons were not statistically significant.

record.summary: This three-arm randomized trial evaluated 14 sessions of group cognitive behavioural therapy in adults with chronic fatigue syndrome, comparing large and small therapy groups with a waiting list. At the second assessment, group CBT significantly improved fatigue, overall impairment, physical functioning, and psychological distress versus waiting list, with large effects for fatigue and impairment.

summary: In adults with chronic fatigue syndrome, 13 sessions of cognitive behavior therapy were compared with relaxation therapy in a randomized trial followed for 5 years. Cognitive behavior therapy produced significantly better long-term global improvement, fewer relapses, more complete recovery, and more weekly work hours, although many patients remained fatigued and the study was affected by follow-up attrition and additional treatments.

summary: This double-blind placebo-controlled trial evaluated three monthly intravenous infusions of high-dose immunoglobulin in 33 patients with chronic fatigue syndrome. Depression improvement was 9.2% with immunoglobulin versus -9.7% with placebo, while immune measure changes did not differ significantly between groups; however, improvement in depression correlated with CD4 and DTH improvement after immunotherapy.

record.summary: In this 22-adolescent randomized pilot trial, four weeks of progressive resistance training was compared with graded aerobic exercise training during an inpatient chronic fatigue rehabilitation programme. Both groups improved exercise capacity, SF-36 physical quality of life, sit-to-stand performance, and depressive symptoms; fatigue severity improved significantly only with aerobic training. No between-group difference was statistically significant.

study_design.randomization_method: Treatment order was allocated randomly and counterbalanced across six possible sequences using a randomization list generated by Papworth Hospital pharmacy.

source_design_and_timing.design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, three-period crossover.
source_design_and_timing.sequence: Six possible treatment sequences, randomly assigned in counterbalanced order using a Papworth Hospital pharmacy randomization list.
source_design_and_timing.treatment_period: 20 days, extendable to a maximum of 26 days for sleep-laboratory scheduling.
source_design_and_timing.washout: Two 14-day washout periods, one between each treatment period.
source_design_and_timing.pharmacokinetics: Modafinil steady state reported as 2-4 days; 14-day washout described as 3.5 times the longest presumed steady-state period.
source_design_and_timing.blinding: Identical capsules and equal capsule counts per day; patients, examiner and clinical staff blinded. Codes would be disclosed only for medical emergency; none occurred.
source_design_and_timing.assessment_schedule: Each visit comprised sleep-laboratory admission the evening before, one day of physiological/clinical/safety assessment, a sleep-laboratory night, and one day of cognitive testing.
source_design_and_timing.cognitive_testing: Started at 09:30 h and lasted approximately 1.75 hours; dosing at 07:30 h, approximately 2 hours before testing.
source_design_and_timing.test_order: Tasks counterbalanced across patients except Motor Screening always first and RVIP always last; parallel versions used where possible.
source_design_and_timing.baseline_cognitive_testing: No formal baseline cognitive testing; MMSE provided an estimate of global cognitive functioning.
source_design_and_timing.carryover: Washout was intended to minimize carryover; authors noted washout was shorter than treatment period and therefore baseline values were not recommended for variability assessment under the cited guidance.

source_dose_and_delivery.placebo: Formulated by DHP Ltd, Powys, UK.
source_dose_and_delivery.modafinil: Cephalon Inc., West Chester, PA, USA.
source_dose_and_delivery.titration: Dose increased every 3 days, starting with one capsule containing 100 mg or placebo, until target dose.
source_dose_and_delivery.administration: Divided morning and noon doses; dosing at 07:30 and 12:00 h on Day 1 and at 07:30 h on Day 2.
source_dose_and_delivery.capsules: Identical appearance and equal number of capsules per day regardless of dose.
source_dose_and_delivery.testing_timing: Cognitive testing began 2 hours after ingestion; expected peak plasma concentration 2-4 hours after oral ingestion.
source_dose_and_delivery.compliance_calculation: (tablets taken / expected tablets taken) × 100; tablets taken = total tablets minus returned tablets.

outcomes.name: RVIP latency to correct detections
outcomes.synthesis_population: Adults meeting Fukuda criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome

source_narrative.result: Patients were significantly quicker on modafinil.

panels: A: each patient's RVIP latency to correct detections, placebo versus 200 mg modafinil
B: each patient's RVIP number of missed targets, placebo versus 400 mg modafinil
figures.annotations: 45-degree equality line. In A, points below the line indicate higher placebo latency and therefore quicker modafinil performance. In B, points above the line indicate more missed targets on modafinil and therefore worse modafinil performance.

panels: A: each patient's SOC mean initial thinking time for two-move problems, placebo versus 200 mg modafinil
B: each patient's SOC mean initial thinking time for five-move problems, placebo versus 400 mg modafinil
figures.annotations: 45-degree equality line. In A, points above the line indicate slower modafinil performance. In B, points below the line indicate quicker modafinil performance.

panels: A: each patient's Trail-Making Test Part B completion time, placebo versus 400 mg modafinil
B: each patient's preferred-hand Finger Tapping mean number of taps, placebo versus 400 mg modafinil
figures.annotations: 45-degree equality line. In A, points above the line indicate slower modafinil performance. In B, points below the line indicate worse modafinil performance because modafinil produced fewer taps.

panels: Each patient's weight, placebo versus 200 mg modafinil
figures.annotations: Points below the equality line indicate higher weight on placebo.
corresponding_narrative_statistics: Z=2.0, p<0.05; mean difference=0.5 kg; SEM=0.4 kg

reported_results.note: Period-adjusted paired rank test; no independent-arm mean effect inferred. Plot coordinates unavailable.

model_tests.test: Period-adjusted within-person Wilcoxon-based comparison
model_tests.analysis_population: 14 completers

record.summary: In adults with CFS, 12 weeks of graded exercise therapy plus standard medical care was compared with standard medical care alone. Exercise significantly reduced physical, mental, and total fatigue at treatment completion, while the physical-functioning difference was not statistically significant; improvements in physical fatigue were maintained at six months.

Numeric data for six-month physical fatigue, mental fatigue, and physical functioning were presented only in Figure 1 and could not be extracted. Table 4 Personal control follow-up SDs appear without parentheses in the source text. Physiological outcome sample sizes were not explicitly stated; the paper reports incomplete data, with ten patients refusing retesting, five invalid maximal-effort tests, and two equipment failures. Table 3 additionally reports current-study total fatigue 13.91 (10.88), SF-36 physical functioning 69.05 (21.94), and Fulcher and White comparator values 20.50 (8.90) and 69.00 (18.50), respectively; comparator-study data were not included as trial-arm outcomes.

record.summary: In this three-arm randomized trial of adults with CFS/ME, pragmatic rehabilitation and supportive listening were compared with treatment as usual. EQ5D health-state distributions improved at week 20 but generally moved toward baseline by week 70; adjusted QALY and cost differences were uncertain, with all reported confidence intervals crossing zero.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: EQ5D mean index values were presented only in Figure 2 and are not numerically extractable here. Table 4 reports adjusted incremental QALYs and costs versus treatment as usual for imputed and complete-case analyses.

record.summary: In adults with CFS/ME treated in primary care, pragmatic rehabilitation, supportive listening and treatment as usual were compared over 70 weeks. In the complete-case analysis, pragmatic rehabilitation produced slightly higher QALYs than treatment as usual, but the incremental benefit was small and uncertain; its cost-effectiveness ratio was £39,583 per QALY. Supportive listening was more costly without greater effectiveness.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This source section contains no outcome tables or per-arm means, SDs, or analyzed Ns. It reports complete-case N=254, an incremental PR-versus-TAU cost of £475 and QALY difference of 0.012 used to calculate the ICER, and cost-effectiveness probabilities of 0.645, 0.626 and 0.600 for TAU at £20,000, £30,000 and £50,000 per QALY. Table 4 is referenced but not included in the supplied section.

source_narrative.caution: The report does not provide event counts, severity, duration, or systematic harms ascertainment; absence of reported significant adverse events must not be interpreted as zero harms.

adverse_events.withdrawal_interpretation: The four withdrawals were explicitly unrelated to intervention. This supports the recorded calculated zero withdrawals due to intervention; it does not imply zero adverse events.

summary: This pilot randomized 39 patients and retained 35 completers. All three tables, the figure and reported harms are retained. Anxiety benefit wording conflicts with the ANOVA interaction result; numerical BAI/BDI means and exact analysis denominators are not reported. Microbiome changes are biomarkers. Synthesis remains pending.

subgroup_analyses.source_quote: Subgrouping according to the 1994 CFS case definition, genotype frequency of the alpha 2A receptor SNP rs1800544 and sex did not reveal any differential response to the intervention. Also, the genotype frequency was equal among CFS patients and healthy controls ( p = 0.75).

summary: NorCAPITAL secondary report of clonidine versus placebo in adolescents with CFS. The flowchart shows 151 initial allocations; 120 participants started treatment and 106 remained at week 8. Tables 3–4 report 41 symptom, catecholamine and autonomic outcomes using last observation carried forward among treatment starters. Adjusted endpoint differences, back-transformed ratios and square-root-transformed results are kept distinct. This report provides no week-30 results. Dose-concentration associations and healthy-control genotyping are separate from randomized treatment effects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Native PDF pages 5–10 verified. Figure 1 adds initial allocation counts and withdrawal reasons absent from the extracted XML caption. All numeric cells in Tables 2–4 are preserved. The authors call the analysis ITT, but 31 initial allocations were not included. Nominal group size 60 differs from observed completers 55/51; exact outcome-specific analyzed counts are not stated. Reported ratios are ratios of back-transformed means.

study_design.design_type_detail: parallel-group, 1:1 randomized, placebo-controlled

arms.label: Clonidine
arms.dose: 50 μg twice daily if body weight >35 kg; 25 μg twice daily if body weight <35 kg

study_design.randomization_method: Computer-based stratified randomization in a 1:1 ratio with block size 4; 18 months disease duration was the stratification criterion.

key_inclusion_criteria: Persisting or constantly relapsing fatigue lasting 3 months or more
Functional disability preventing normal school attendance
Age ≥12 years and <18 years
No other medical or psychiatric disorder explaining the fatigue
key_exclusion_criteria: Another current disease process or demanding life event explaining the fatigue
Permanent use of drugs including hormones
Reduced cerebral or peripheral circulation due to vessel disease

record.summary: This double-blind randomized trial evaluated oral clonidine versus placebo in 120 adolescents with ME/CFS. At week 8, most cardiovascular and autonomic outcomes showed no statistically significant between-group differences; supine LF-HRV power was higher with clonidine, with a ratio of 1.4 (95% CI 1.1 to 1.8; p=0.007).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 4 reports means and model-based between-group contrasts but no SDs or SEs. All calculations used 120 individuals, 60 per arm, with missing values imputed by last observation carried forward. Variables marked * used ln transformation and ratios; variables marked # used square-root transformation, with differences and ratios not applicable.

study_design.design_type_detail: parallel-group, 1:1 randomized, placebo-controlled

arms.label: Clonidine
arms.dose: 50 μg twice daily if body weight >35 kg; 25 μg twice daily if body weight <35 kg

study_design.randomization_method: Computer-based stratified randomization in a 1:1 ratio with block size 4; 18 months disease duration was the stratification criterion.

key_inclusion_criteria: Persisting or constantly relapsing fatigue lasting 3 months or more
Functional disability preventing normal school attendance
Age ≥12 years and <18 years
No other medical or psychiatric disorder explaining the fatigue
key_exclusion_criteria: Another current disease process or demanding life event explaining the fatigue
Permanent use of drugs including hormones
Reduced cerebral or peripheral circulation due to vessel disease
Hypersensitivity to clonidine or capsule substances
Abnormal ECG apart from ectopic beats
Upright systolic blood pressure fall >30 mmHg

record.summary: In adolescents with CFS, low-dose oral clonidine reduced catecholamine levels. Dose-response relationships were statistically significant for urine norepinephrine/creatinine ratio, TPRI, LF-HRV, and HRV-Total Power, while symptoms of orthostatic intolerance were not improved.

healthy_comparison_cohort.source_quote: The genotyping of the alpha 2A receptor single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) rs1800544 was carried out by predesigned TaqMan SNP genotyping assay (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA), using the SDS 2.2 software (Applied Biosystems). As previously described, approximately 10 % of the samples were re-genotyped, and the concordance rate was 100 % [ 27 ]. Genotyping was also performed in 68 healthy individuals having the same distribution of gender and age as the CFS patients.

reported_statistical_methods: Determination of sample size is described elsewhere [ 28 ]. Outcome of clonidine intervention was assessed by general linear models (ANCOVA) in intention-to-treat analyses, including baseline values as covariates in the model [ 37 ]. The net intervention effect was calculated from the parameters of the fitted general linear model. Differential effects in subgroups adhering to the 1994 CFS case definition, genotype of the alpha 2A receptor single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) rs1800544, and sex, were explored by including these variables as interaction terms. Dose–response relationships for patients allocated to clonidine were explored by linear regression analyses. Missing values were imputed as last observation carried forward from the pre-medication test. In order to obtain near-normally distributed variables, ln-transformation was carried out for supine values of LF-HRV, HF-HRV, Total Power-HRV, LF/HF ratio and LF-SBP. Square root transformation was carried out for 20° head-up tilt values of LF-HRV, HF-HRV and Total Power-HRV. Genotype frequency among patients and healthy controls were explored with chi-square analyses.

record.summary: This section reports a LASSO regression distinguishing female CFS/ME patients from healthy controls using protein biomarkers. TWEAK, CCL4, IL12B, CDCP1, VEGFA, and CSF1 had the largest positive weights, while BetaNGF and LIFR had the largest negative weights. The model had an AUC of 0.9996 and corrected AUC of 0.7344; no intervention efficacy results are reported in this section.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Source section contains Table 2 only. It reports conditional LASSO protein weights and model-performance metrics, not per-arm clinical trial outcome means, SDs, sample sizes, or treatment effects. Leading zeros in table weights were preserved numerically as values such as 0865 -> 865; negative values retain their signs. Table footnote states: Given associations are all conditional on the other predictors.

record.summary: In this double-blind randomized trial, female adults with CFS/ME received subcutaneous anakinra or placebo for 4 weeks. Anakinra significantly increased circulating IL-1Ra concentrations (p < 0.001); figure-based analyses suggested effects on CSF-1, IL-18R1, ENRAGE, and CXCL-9, but their numeric estimates were not stated in this section.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Numeric cytokine treatment effects and confidence intervals were available only in Figure 3; the figure itself was not provided. Figure 2 showed a significant IL-1Ra increase with p < 0.001 but no arm-level means or dispersion. One anakinra participant discontinued after 2 weeks due to an adverse event and was excluded.

record.summary: This section reports a LASSO regression distinguishing female CFS/ME patients from healthy controls using protein biomarkers. TWEAK, CCL4, IL12B, CDCP1, VEGFA, and CSF1 had the largest positive weights, while BetaNGF and LIFR had the largest negative weights. The model had an AUC of 0.9996 and corrected AUC of 0.7344; no intervention efficacy results are reported in this section.

record.summary: In this double-blind randomized trial, female adults with CFS/ME received subcutaneous anakinra or placebo for 4 weeks. Anakinra significantly increased circulating IL-1Ra concentrations (p < 0.001); figure-based analyses suggested effects on CSF-1, IL-18R1, ENRAGE, and CXCL-9, but their numeric estimates were not stated in this section.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Numeric cytokine treatment effects and confidence intervals were available only in Figure 3; the figure itself was not provided. Figure 2 showed a significant IL-1Ra increase with p < 0.001 but no arm-level means or dispersion. One anakinra participant discontinued after 2 weeks due to an adverse event and was excluded.

record.summary: In 60 female adults with chronic fatigue syndrome and Spleen-Kidney Yang deficiency, 60-minute Long-snake-like moxibustion was compared with 30-minute treatment for 4 weeks. The 60-minute group had significantly lower end-of-treatment physical fatigue, FS-14 total score, several syndrome symptoms, and syndrome total score, while SDS and SAS did not differ significantly.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Numerical values for TTM outcomes were reported in prose and compared each treatment group with 30 healthy controls; Table 8 was referenced but not included in the supplied section. FS-14 and individual syndrome symptoms were reported as medians and IQRs, not means and SDs.

record.summary: In this assessor-blinded randomized trial, Tuina plus usual care was compared with usual care alone in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome. Tuina significantly improved anxiety, PSQI total score, sleep duration, sleep disturbance, and daytime dysfunction, but not depression, SF-36 bodily pain or physical functioning, subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep efficiency, or sleep medication use. No serious adverse events were reported; two Tuina participants experienced transient local pain.

record.summary: In adults with ME/CFS, a two-month seated isometric yoga intervention added to conventional pharmacotherapy was compared with conventional pharmacotherapy alone. Yoga significantly improved Chalder Fatigue Scale scores and HADS-D scores versus control, while TAS-20 and HADS-A differences were not significant. Biomarker and autonomic outcomes were reported only for the yoga group and showed no clearly significant pre/post changes after multiplicity adjustment.

Table 2 reports change scores for both groups and Cohen’s d, but no arm-specific endpoint means.

record.summary: In adults with ME/CFS and comorbid fibromyalgia, recumbent isometric yoga added to conventional therapy reduced Chalder Fatigue Scale scores from 30.2 ± 2.3 to 23.8 ± 4.8, while control scores changed from 28.3 ± 4.8 to 28.6 ± 4.2. 0.47 and p = 0.13 respectively). Eight subjects were excluded when implementing the modified Kraemer approach because they did not have a match within the set calliper distance of the prognostic score. ## Discussion This paper reported on a comparison of three methods for constructing personalised treatment recommendations from randomised controlled trial data: the regression method that models outcome using treatment by moderator biomarker interactions; a method proposed by Kraemer that forms a combined moderator from individual moderator weights, calculated on all treated and control pairs; and a modification of Kraemer ' s approach that utilises a prognostic score to sample pairs of treated and control subjects. Across all simulations, the regression approach outperformed Kraemer ' s approach. The modification of Kraemer ' s approach appeared to indicate higher values of θ , except in the case where there was a strong unobserved prognostic marker. The superiority of the regression approach was replicated using real-world data from a randomised trial of home-delivered pragmatic rehabilitation for chronic fatigue patients; however, for this example, no method conclusively demonstrated that a PTR does better than a policy of ' treatment as usual ' despite there being several individual moderators of treatment effect [13]. Therefore, in this case, we conclude that forming a PTR is more difficult than finding individual treatment effect moderators. All three methods described here use linear parameterisation to model trial data, and therefore, the efficacy of these methods relies on the models being correctly specified. In many situations, non-linear models may be more applicable and when there are many variables then the likelihood of correctly specifying the model might be low. For example, none of the approaches, on average, indicated an improvement under PTR in the scenario with a non-linear data-generating model. These simulations were limited because they did not include any variable selection or transformations of variables based on model fit. Such processes require care and often require knowledge of the variables at hand. In practice, researchers will be insuring against model underfitting by testing for non-linear terms and higher-order interactions. Overfitting of these models could be counterbalanced using regularisation techniques, such as Lasso regression. Additionally, methods exist that are more robust to model misspecification, for example methods that seek to maximise the expected outcome under a PTR using classification techniques [14 -16]. The application to the FINE randomised control trial showed that a PTR, as estimated using the regression approach, might result in an improvement over a recommendation where everybody is provided treatment as usual; however, the 95% confidence interval for all approaches included estimates where the PTR strategy is associated with a small amount of harm. These results should not be over-interpreted: the 95% confidence intervals were wide, which indicates insufficient power to detect a change. Data from another trial testing the use of the PTR would be needed to confirm whether any PTR results in an overall benefit. Another aspect that should be considered is whether including cost information in the measure of benefit has an effect on the decision to adopt a PTR strategy. In the discussion to the paper, Kraemer says: ' an irrelevant baseline factor and a non-specific predictor can have no influence on making different choices between [treatments] ' . We argue that this appears to be false, based on our findings: information from a prognostic score appears to result in a composite moderator that more effectively discriminates between those who should receive treatment and those that should not. Whilst the Kraemer approach does not appear to improve on the regression approach, it should be noted that the original paper provides a useful example of how to judge the relative effect sizes of multiple modifiers that would form a useful exploratory analysis before forming a PTR. ## Conclusion Our simulations demonstrate that the parametric method proposed by Kraemer does not result in a more effective personalised treatment recommendation than a method that uses a regression model. Utilising a prognostic score improves the Kraemer method, however not to an extent that it should be adopted over the regression method. ## Abbreviations PTR: Personalised treatment recommendation; RCT: Randomised controlled trial; FINE: Fatigue Intervention Nurses Evaluation randomised trial ## Acknowledgements We would like to thank Alison Wearden and the rest of the FINE team for the use of their trial data and Andrew Pickles and Jennifier Hellier for their helpful comments on this work. record.summary: Adults with long COVID and chronic fatigue syndrome were randomized to hospital-based rehabilitation, telerehabilitation, or a home programme for 8 weeks. Hospital-based rehabilitation produced the largest improvement in SF-36 physical functioning, while both rehabilitation approaches improved DALYs relative to home exercise; several respiratory and physiological outcomes also showed statistically significant omnibus or pairwise differences.

Some reported p-values appear internally inconsistent with the stated significance conclusions.

summary: This 2x2 factorial randomized trial evaluated six months of graded exercise and fixed-dose fluoxetine in adults meeting Oxford criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome. Graded exercise significantly improved functional work capacity at 12 and 26 weeks and reduced case-level fatigue at 26 weeks, while fluoxetine produced a modest, transient improvement in depression at week 12 only.

The paper reports factorial main effects rather than complete pairwise arm-level contrasts.

record.summary: This randomized trial compared three therapist-contact doses of an educational psychological intervention encouraging home-based graded exercise in patients with Oxford-criteria chronic fatigue syndrome. All treatment groups improved, with no significant difference between treatment dosages; poorer physical-functioning and handicap outcomes were associated mainly with dysphoria, support-group membership, and sickness-benefit receipt.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The report is a predictor analysis of three treated randomized arms and excludes the 34-patient no-treatment control group. Most outcome means and SDs are reported only for the treated cohort overall, not separately by arm. Table 3 contains standardized regression coefficients, t statistics, and P values; coefficients are preserved as model-based effects. Text encoding renders minus signs as 7 and less-than signs as 5 in several locations.

record.summary: In adults meeting Oxford criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome, a patient-education intervention promoting graded exercise and sleep regulation produced sustained improvements in physical functioning and fatigue through 2 years. The three active treatment dosages did not differ significantly, while patients treated after a 1-year waiting period had poorer fatigue outcomes and lower recovery rates.

record.summary: In this three-arm randomized trial of adults with CFS, protocol-driven and feedback-on-demand internet CBT were compared with a waiting list over 6 months. Both iCBT formats significantly reduced fatigue severity and improved several secondary outcomes versus waiting list, with no significant efficacy difference between iCBT formats. Feedback-on-demand required significantly less therapist time.

summary: This randomized primary-care trial compared 18 weeks of home-based pragmatic rehabilitation with general practitioner treatment as usual among adults with chronic fatigue syndrome. Pragmatic rehabilitation improved fatigue overall, but higher baseline depressive symptoms and total HADS scores significantly moderated the effect, with smaller improvements among participants with more depressive symptoms.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The report analyzes pragmatic rehabilitation versus treatment as usual, although the parent trial had three arms including supportive listening. Table 3 contains OCR-garbled minus signs rendered as 7; these were interpreted as negative signs. Table 2 reports arm-level fatigue means and SDs at baseline, 20 weeks, and 70 weeks. Per-arm randomized totals and detailed attrition are not reported for the two-arm comparison.

summary: This double-blind crossover study evaluated 28 days of low-dose oral hydrocortisone versus placebo in medication-free adults with CFS. Hydrocortisone did not significantly alter serum IGF measures, GH responses to insulin stress or GHRH, or IGFBP-1 suppression; urinary GH decreased during both hydrocortisone and placebo periods.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The study reports a crossover hydrocortisone trial in 37 CFS patients, with dynamic endocrine outcomes assessed in subsets of 15 or 16 participants. Several GH response curves contain figure-only time-course data; only text- and table-reported summary values were extracted. Table 4 contains apparent typographical errors in the baseline urinary GH IQR (33.0-17.9); the values were preserved as printed.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Nine of 32 patients were categorized as treatment responders; responders had a significant increase in cortisol response to human CRH, but numeric subgroup values are not provided.
No significant differences were apparent in male or female subgroups; observed differences were in the same direction as the overall group.

record.summary: This double-blind crossover trial tested 28-day oral low-dose hydrocortisone, 5 or 10 mg daily, versus placebo in adults with CFS. Overall treatment effects on endocrine challenge responses were not numerically presented in the supplied text, although urinary free cortisol was higher after active treatment and nine of 32 participants met the fatigue-response definition. At baseline, patients had lower urinary free cortisol and reduced cortisol responses relative to ACTH responses compared with healthy controls.

Baseline CFS-versus-healthy-control table values were retained, but these observational comparison groups do not correspond to the randomized hydrocortisone/placebo treatment arms; arm IDs are therefore a schema-compatible representation rather than true treatment-arm assignments. Figure-only time-course values were not extracted.

title: Hypothalamo-Pituitary-Adrenal Axis Dysfunction in Chronic Fatigue Syndrome, and the Effects of Low-Dose Hydrocortisone Therapy
authors: Cleare AJ; Miell J.; Heap E.; Sookdeo S.; Young L.; Malhi GS; O'Keane V.
journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism

release_limitations.reason: Numerical conclusions are withheld until unresolved source coverage and reconciliation findings are reviewed.

study_design.design_type_detail: parallel-group, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled
study_design.randomization_method: Block randomization

source_design_and_timing.design: Multi-center, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled parallel-group clinical trial.
source_design_and_timing.diagnostic_framework: CFS or ICF according to CDC 1994 criteria.
source_design_and_timing.planned_sample_size: 27 per group sufficient for a one-point mean-change FSS difference, power=80%, α=0.05; 39 per group planned assuming 30% withdrawal.
source_design_and_timing.assessments: Physical condition, vital signs, fatigue severity, serious life events and AEs checked at week 3; laboratory tests, fatigue severity, serious life events and AEs checked after 6 weeks.
source_design_and_timing.blinding: Opaque film covered syringes because HPE was slightly opaque yellowish brown and saline was colorless.

scales.FSS: 9 items, each scored 1–7; score is average of items.
scales.MFI: 20-item instrument; general, physical and mental fatigue, reduced motivation and reduced activity; items scored 1–5; subscales 4–20; total 20–100; higher scores indicate greater fatigue.

source_dose_and_delivery.treatment: Human placental extract, Laennec®, Lot No. 30405, manufactured by GCJBP Corporation, Yongin, Korea.
source_dose_and_delivery.comparator: Normal saline, Lot No. 30402, 4 mL per injection, three times weekly for 6 weeks.
source_dose_and_delivery.product_description: HPE described as an aqueous human-placenta hydrolysate containing proteins of MW 10–100 kDa, minerals, amino acids and steroid hormones.
source_dose_and_delivery.manufacturing_details_omitted: Laboratory production, raw-material processing, sterilization and pathogen-testing procedures omitted as requested.

source_limitations: Small sample and 6-week follow-up; long-term efficacy and safety cannot be assessed.
Subjective fatigue outcomes may be influenced by emotional state and placebo effects.
No objective functional, employment, activity or quality-of-life endpoint was reported.
Subgroup numerical data for ICF and total CF were not provided.
No multiplicity adjustment for multiple outcomes and subgroup analyses was reported.
No confidence intervals, effect sizes or missing-data handling were reported.
Sponsor funding and conflicts: study supported by Green Cross Corporation and GCJBP Corporation; all authors received a research grant from these companies.
The reported AE categories are summarized by percentage and count, but individual event terms, severity, timing and relatedness are not provided.
The article does not provide a supplementary appendix or participant-level dataset.
MFI change-comparison P.0159 in abstract and endpoint-comparison P.0200 in Results refer to different estimands,not a contradiction. Exact analyzed subgroup Ns unavailable.
source_contradictions: VAS Methods andFigure2 use0–10 while Table1/narrative values are around70; scale/unit presentation differs and values are not silently rescaled.
MFI Methods describes20–100 total and4–20 subscales; reported means around2–3 andFigure2C1–5 axis indicate another score metric that is not explicitly defined.
MFI narrative calls2.28/2.70 decreases,but Figure2C and baseline comparison identify them as endpoints. Baselines2.85/2.99 retained; no MFI change SD inferred.
Table2 printed changes often do not equal displayed endpoint minus baseline; e.g. platelet placebo232.74→233.41 but change−1.38. Missing-data populations could differ but are not explained.
Laboratory narrative calls hemoglobin whereas Tables1/2 label hematocrit; retain the printed analyte without conversion.

source_narrative_results.population: 78 randomized subjects with chronic fatigue; HPE n=39 and placebo n=39
source_narrative_results.result: At baseline, FSS, VAS and MFI did not differ between groups. HPE was reported to improve fatigue in the CFS subgroup but not the ICF subgroup after 6 weeks.
All reported baseline clinical, blood-pressure, biochemical and fatigue comparisons were nonsignificant; subgroup baseline values were stated to be nonsignificantly different but not shown.

source_narrative_results.population: CFS subgroup; flow diagram shows HPE/Laennec n=19 and placebo n=21
results: FSS baseline/end: HPE 5.29±0.91 to 3.24±1.28, within-group p<0.0001; placebo 5.13±0.82 to 4.09±1.22, within-group p=0.0016.
FSS mean change: HPE −2.05±1.43 versus placebo −1.04±1.30; between-group p=0.0242, unpaired t-test.
VAS mean change: HPE −36.21±26.20 versus placebo −13.33±17.16; between-group p=0.0009, unpaired t-test.
MFI baseline2.85±.47/2.99±.61; endpoint2.28±.57/2.70±.52,consistent with Figure2C. Text calls endpoint values decreases; this wording is retained as a source ambiguity. Within-group P<.0001/.0004.
End-of-study group comparisons: FSS p=0.0378, VAS p=0.0052, MFI p=0.0200.

source_narrative_results.result: No significant between-group differences in mean change from baseline for FSS, VAS or MFI; numerical results were not provided.
No statistically significant between-group differences in change from baseline for SBP, DBP, WBC, hematocrit, platelet count, AST, ALT, total bilirubin, FBG, BUN or creatinine.
No process or predictor associations, regression models, correlations, mediation analyses or carryover analyses were reported.
Discussion proposed anti-inflammatory and immune-related mechanisms, citing prior studies; these were not outcomes of the present randomized trial.
No significant between-group changes in FSS,VAS or MFI in all CF subjects; numeric results not shown.

source_companion_notes: No supplements or companion reports were supplied or identified in the provided source.
References cited by the article are external background studies, not additional randomized evidence from this trial.

summary: In this randomized, double-blind pilot trial, 12 adults meeting CDC criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome received oral guanidinoacetic acid 2.4 g/day or cellulose placebo for four weeks. GAA significantly improved the MFI-20 outcome compared with placebo (p=0.02), and health-related quality of life and muscular strength also improved between groups (p<0.05), although detailed values were not reported.

record.summary: This randomized pilot trial compared 12 weeks of graded cycling and intermittent cycling with usual care in adults with CFS, with a non-CFS control group. Both exercise programs improved several exercise-capacity and immune-cell outcomes, but fatigue severity remained high and did not differ significantly between groups.

record.summary: This trial evaluated oral galanthamine hydrobromide in adults meeting consensus criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome. Galanthamine-treated patients showed statistically significant within-treatment improvements in sleep disturbance, fatigue, myalgia, memory, delayed recall, trait anxiety, cognitive failures, and cortisol, although the optional crossover design, treatment switching, adverse effects, and lack of reported direct between-group estimates substantially limit confidence in the findings.

record.summary: This double-blind randomized crossover study tested oral galanthamine hydrobromide in adults meeting consensus criteria for CFS, with fatigue, sleep disturbance and myalgia assessed using visual analogue scales. Among 33 protocol completers, 43% reported more than 50% improvement in the main symptoms and 70% reported more than 30% improvement; over 60% reported more than 70% improvement in sleep deficit. Arm-specific means, standard deviations and between-group effect estimates were not reported in this source section.

narrative_results.finding: Of the 49 recruited patients, five did not progress beyond week two for non-treatment-related reasons; 24 changed to alternative therapy by the end of week two.

narrative_results.finding: All galanthamine-treated patients, including those initially allocated to galanthamine and those transferred from placebo, showed highly significant improvement by week 8 in sleep disturbance, fatigue and myalgia, each p < 0.001.
additional_results: Work capacity/satisfaction improved by week 4, p < 0.01, but the improvement was reversed by week 8, p < 0.162.
Memory and dizziness changes were nonsignificant.
No differences or trend differences were seen between maximum-dose Group A (30 mg and above) and Group B (20 mg or less) at baseline, weeks 1, 2, 4 or 8.

narrative_results.finding: State anxiety changes at eight weeks fell short of significance, p = 0.055. Trait anxiety changed significantly after the first week and was highly significant after eight weeks, p < 0.001.

Immediate logical memory improved significantly after eight weeks, p < 0.01; delayed logical material improved highly significantly after eight weeks, p < 0.001. Cognitive failures were significantly reduced beyond four weeks, p < 0.05.
No significant changes in hematological, liver, or renal function tests were noted.

Thirty-two patients had random, late-morning blood cortisol levels at baseline and at the fourth and fifth visits. Nineteen started in active treatment and 16 in placebo; by the fourth visit all were on galanthamine. Cortisol showed a significant intra-patient rise, p < 0.002; pre-treatment 231.91 nmol/l and post-treatment 320.44 nmol/l, with standard deviations 116.87 and 117.78.

Among 33 patients reported in the Discussion as finishing according to protocol, 43% reported over 50% decrease in fatigue, sleep disturbance and myalgia, and 70% reported over 30% improvement. Over 60% of patients who finished reported over 70% improvement in sleep deficit.
Only one patient on placebo improved over 10% during the first two weeks.

Tables 10 and 11 report lifetime psychiatric diagnoses, whereas trial exclusion criteria used actual diagnosis at the time of the trial. Table 10 compares the Icelandic CFS group with a general-population epidemiological survey; Table 11 compares it with an American CFS group. These are external comparisons, not randomized treatment outcomes.

other_source_issues: Narrative on page 12 states WMS data were available at baseline and after 6 and 8 weeks, while Tables 6 and 7 report baseline, 4 Weeks, and 8 Weeks.
Narrative on page 12 refers to changes after 4 weeks and 8 weeks despite the preceding 6- and 8-week statement.
Narrative on page 13 states CFQ data were available at baseline and after 6 and 8 weeks, while Table 8 reports baseline, 4 Weeks, and 8 Weeks.
Narrative on page 13 states that 32 patients had cortisol levels taken at baseline and at the fourth and fifth visits; Table 9 does not print an N.
Narrative on page 14 states that 19 patients started in the active treatment group and 16 in the placebo group, with all on galanthamine by the fourth visit; these are not Table 9 cell values.
Tables represent pooled all-galanthamine groups after optional crossover, not randomized arm contrasts.
The supplied narrative contains OCR/transcription artifacts and typographical inconsistencies, including DSM-III/DISIIIA, DSM-III-R, CFS/CPS, and varying reported completion counts.
The abstract reports 39 protocol completers, while the Discussion reports 33; Table 3 reports N=40 at baseline and N=32 at eight weeks.
The abstract says improvement reached significance after four to eight weeks; the Discussion says after four to six weeks.
Table 10 is described in the narrative as a comparison to Katon et al. (25), while the printed Table 10 footnote attributes it to Stefansson et al. 1991 (25); Table 11 cites Katon et al. 1991 (26).
Table 10 and Table 11 are lifetime-diagnosis comparisons and include general-population and American CFS historical data; they must not be attributed as trial treatment results.
The source states that 30% of patients had active-drug adverse effects, which could compromise the double blind.

The source states that 70% followed the escalating dosage schedule and 30% had dosage reduced because of adverse effects, mainly nausea; no participant-level denominator is printed for the 30% harm statement.
No unprinted values, standard deviations, treatment effects, zero harms, or plot coordinates were inferred.

summary: In this small randomized trial of 20 adults with chronic fatigue syndrome, twice-weekly massage therapy for five weeks was compared with sham TENS tactile stimulation. Massage produced significantly greater immediate reductions in depression, anxiety, pain, and salivary cortisol, and greater five-week improvements in depression, fatigue-related symptoms, pain, sleep, urinary cortisol, and dopamine. Standard deviations and exact effect estimates were not reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Tables report raw means only; the paper states that standard deviations can be obtained from the author. The source text contains OCR/conversion artifacts in several F statistics and p-value strings. No participant-level analyzed Ns, attrition, adverse events, confidence intervals, or direct between-group effect estimates were reported.

record.summary: In this small randomized trial of 20 adults with chronic fatigue syndrome, twice-weekly massage therapy for five weeks was compared with sham TENS tactile stimulation. Massage produced significantly greater immediate reductions in depression, anxiety, pain, and salivary cortisol, and greater five-week improvements in depression, fatigue-related symptoms, pain, sleep, urinary cortisol, and dopamine. Standard deviations and exact effect estimates were not reported.

summary: This double-blind placebo-controlled trial evaluated intravenous gammaglobulin, 1 g/kg monthly for three months, in adolescents with CFS. At six months, anergic participants receiving gammaglobulin had better functional scores and greater functional improvement than placebo recipients, but the five-year difference was not statistically significant. Overall, participants generally continued to improve, although a substantial minority remained impaired.

record.summary: This small single-blind randomized trial evaluated oral Isoprinosine versus methylcellulose placebo in adults with chronic fatigue syndrome. At week 12, Isoprinosine was associated with higher NK-cell activity and CD4-cell counts in the clinically Improved subgroup, while cognitive, Karnofsky, and tender-point outcomes were not significantly different between groups. Extended treatment was associated with increased IL-12 production and CD4+ HLA-DR+ cells at week 28.

summary: This small controlled pilot study evaluated one week of hyperbaric oxygen therapy in adults with CDC 1994 CFS, comparing patients with Mycoplasma hominis infection with those without infection. Mycoplasma-infected participants showed numerical improvements in fatigue, activity, bodily pain, and some cognitive measures, but the reported omnibus interaction p-values were generally non-significant except for bodily pain (p=.010).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Only six outcomes were retained to meet the requested size limit. Omitted numerically reported outcomes include MFI Physical Fatigue, Reduced Motivation, Mental Fatigue; GHQ-30; CGHQ-30; SF-36 Physical Functioning, General Health Perceptions, Vitality, Social Functioning, Role-Emotional; and reaction-time measures SRTR, SRTL, CRT, CRTS, CRr2, CRTD, CRTR, CRTF, SRTr3. Table 4 reports only baseline and 1-month values. Figure 1 contains no extractable numeric values beyond Table 3.

record.summary: This pilot study evaluated one week of hyperbaric oxygen therapy in adults with chronic fatigue syndrome, reporting separate paired results for Mycoplasma hominis-infected and non-infected patients. In infected patients, fatigue, activity, general health, role-physical functioning, and reaction-time scores changed at selected assessments, while non-infected patients showed a reported mental-health change; no between-group effects were reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Only Tables 5 and 6 were available in this source section. Tables report paired within-group mean (SD) values and P values, but do not report sample sizes or between-group effect estimates. Numeric data for Bodily Pain and other context-listed outcomes were not present in this section.

summary: This double-blind randomized trial tested 14 weeks of oral Acclydine plus amino acid supplementation versus placebo in adults with CDC-defined CFS and elevated IGFBP3/IGF1 ratios. Acclydine did not significantly improve fatigue severity or functional impairment, and no significant effects were found for activity, daily fatigue, or hormonal outcomes.

record.summary: This double-blind randomized trial tested intravenous rituximab against saline placebo in adults with Fukuda-defined ME/CFS. Rituximab produced greater maximum changes in SF-36 physical function and bodily pain, with statistically significant between-group p-values of 0.014 and 0.005, respectively; other SF-36 changes were not statistically significant.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 4 reports baseline SF-36 values for n=13 in the rituximab group and n=15 in the placebo group; maximum changes are percentages with SDs and no reported mean differences or confidence intervals. Table 5 reports adverse-event counts, with some zero cells lacking percentages.

record.summary: In adults with debilitating CFS/ME, rintatolimod was compared with placebo in a double-blind randomized trial followed by a blinded crossover extension. During Stage 1, rintatolimod improved ADL and vitality scores and reduced concomitant medication use, while the placebo group showed smaller or nonsignificant changes; adverse events were common in both groups, with several symptoms more frequent with rintatolimod.

record.summary: This double-blind randomized trial tested intravenous rintatolimod versus placebo in 234 adults with severe CFS/ME. At week 40, rintatolimod improved treadmill exercise tolerance more than placebo in the ITT population, with a statistically significant placebo-adjusted benefit (p=0.047), and more patients achieved at least 25% or 50% improvement.

record.summary: In adults with debilitating CFS/ME, rintatolimod was compared with placebo in a double-blind randomized trial followed by a blinded crossover extension. During Stage 1, rintatolimod improved ADL and vitality scores and reduced concomitant medication use, while the placebo group showed smaller or nonsignificant changes; adverse events were common in both groups, with several symptoms more frequent with rintatolimod.

record.summary: In severely debilitated adults with CFS/ME, rintatolimod significantly improved treadmill exercise tolerance compared with placebo at week 40. Placebo-adjusted improvement was 21.3% (p=0.047), with larger corrected improvement of 28% (p=0.022); responder proportions also favored rintatolimod. Rintatolimod reduced concomitant medication use versus placebo (68% vs 55%, p=0.048).

CBT and GET produced better fatigue and disability outcomes than specialist care, while CBT improved QALYs significantly versus specialist care; CBT also had lower societal costs than adaptive pacing.

record.summary: This secondary analysis compared pragmatic rehabilitation with supportive listening in adults with CFS/ME. Pragmatic rehabilitation produced significantly greater improvement in fatigue and physical functioning at 20 weeks, but differences were not statistically significant at 70 weeks. Therapist-associated effects were generally small, while therapeutic alliance varied by therapist.

record.summary: In this post-hoc analysis of the randomized, double-blind AMP-516 Phase III trial, 40 weeks of rintatolimod improved exercise tolerance more than placebo in the 2–8-year Target Subset, with a 61.9-foot between-group difference at the threshold of significance (p=0.050). Rintatolimod-treated responders also showed clinically relevant improvements in Vitality Score and Karnofsky Performance Scale, while Non-Target Subset exercise differences were not statistically significant.

record.summary: This double-blind randomized substudy evaluated rituximab versus placebo saline in adults with ME/CFS. summary: In this follow-up of adolescents with CFS, CBT was associated with sustained reductions in fatigue and improved physical functioning and school/work attendance over approximately 2 years. Compared with adolescents who did not receive CBT, the CBT group had significantly better follow-up fatigue, physical functioning, and attendance outcomes, although the long-term comparison was nonrandomized and affected by crossover and missing data.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The report combines the original randomized CBT group with waiting-list participants who later chose CBT; long-term CBT versus no-treatment analyses are as-treated and nonrandomized. Table 1 contains within-group postwaiting-list/posttreatment outcomes for 18 subsequently treated participants. Follow-up mean values in Table 2 use n = 50 for CBT and n = 16 for no treatment, while attendance analyses use n = 42 and n = 12.

summary: In adolescents meeting CDC criteria for CFS, Internet-based CBT through FITNET was compared with usual care in a randomized trial with later crossover and approximately 2.7 years of follow-up. Recovery remained favorable in both pathways, with 64% in the direct FITNET group and 53.6% in the usual-care-only group at LTFU; the reported comparisons were not statistically significant (P=.251 and P=.515).

summary: This open-label randomized trial enrolled 38 adults with verified chronic fatigue syndrome and compared five weeks of intravenous human placenta extract Laennec with a control group. Laennec was associated with statistically significant improvements in chronic fatigue, depression, several SF-36 domains, exercise capacity, and lipid measures, although the absence of placebo control and blinding substantially limits confidence in these findings.

Control-group 5-week follow-up values were generally represented as dashes. The paper reports within-group p-values but no explicit between-group effect estimates.

summary: This randomized trial compared ginger-indirect moxibustion plus acupuncture with acupuncture alone in 276 adults with chronic fatigue syndrome. Both groups improved, but the combined treatment produced statistically significant additional improvement in FSS from week 4 through week 20 and in SPHERE from week 2 through week 20; SDS and HAMA differences were not statistically significant.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 reports numeric change-from-baseline values with SDs at weeks 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, and 20; raw follow-up endpoints are not reported. Table 2 HTML has merged cells and lacks explicit outcome labels on some rows, so rows were mapped using the table ordering and captions. The paper states 12 adverse events, 8 in Group A and 4 in Group B, but does not clearly allocate each listed event by arm.

record.summary: In adults with chronic fatigue syndrome, a 7-day waterfall forest environment intervention was compared with an urban environment. Waterfall forest exposure produced lower day-7 somatic and mental fatigue scores, with reported between-group significance at P<0.01. Baseline psychophysiological measures were generally well matched between groups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Numeric mood-scale results after intervention were presented only in Figure 7 and were not extractable from the supplied text. Table 7 also reports additional baseline measures including waistline, blood pressure, cholesterol, triglyceride, creatinine, sleep time, beverage intake, drug abuse and exercise; these were not represented as clinical outcomes.

summary: This double-blind randomized trial tested single-session intramuscular lidocaine injections versus saline in adults with CFS. Lidocaine reduced overall fatigue significantly more than saline at 30 minutes (p = 0.03), while the between-group difference in pain was not significant; depression and anxiety declined over time without differential treatment effects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Numerical fatigue and pain means and SDs were available only in Figures 1 and 2, whose graphical values were not provided in the supplied text. Table 2 was referenced but not included in the supplied XML. The reported ANOVA statistics were extracted.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: Only 86 of 114 participants had baseline and 12-month physical-functioning data, and analyses used post hoc improved versus non-improved subgroups.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Participants were classified by changes from baseline to 12 months: non-improved changed 5 to -35 points; improved changed 10 to 55 points.
Positive change occurred in 63% of the low/moderate activity group versus 29% of the high activity group.

summary: This randomized study evaluated several non-pharmacologic interventions in adults with Fukuda-defined CFS, but this report primarily examined predictors of 12-month physical-functioning improvement. Improvement was associated with higher baseline SF-36 functioning at follow-up, lower B-cell measures, greater perceived energy, less expended energy, less sleep dysfunction, and more baseline work activity; many subgroup differences were statistically significant. The analysis was exploratory and limited by substantial missing follow-up data and post hoc responder grouping.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The report lists five treatment protocols but states that participants were assigned to four conditions and does not provide treatment-arm-specific outcome data. Most numeric results compare post hoc improved versus non-improved subgroups; subgroup sample sizes and SDs are not reported. The text reports 114 enrolled participants, 86 with baseline and follow-up physical-functioning data, and 24 additional screened individuals excluded.

record.summary: This three-arm randomized trial compared two stepped-care formats using internet-based CBT, with face-to-face CBT when needed, against treatment as usual in adults with chronic fatigue syndrome. Both stepped-care formats were noninferior to treatment as usual for fatigue, with no significant differences in secondary outcomes or clinically significant improvement rates.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Among 95 patients receiving f2f CBT after I-CBT, fatigue severity, SIP8, and SF-36 physical functioning improved significantly; SCL-90 did not.

record.summary: Among patients with chronic fatigue syndrome receiving stepped care, those who proceeded from I-CBT to face-to-face CBT showed significant additional improvement in fatigue severity, disability, and physical functioning, but not psychological distress. Symptom scores appeared to improve more with supplementation, but treatment effects were not statistically significant for PQ, GHQ, or SUM at 3 months, and the 6-month GHQ treatment effect had P=0.19.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Numeric outcome values were primarily presented in Figures 4-10 as means ± 2 SEM and were not tabulated or stated in the text, so per-arm follow-up means and dispersions are unavailable. Reported descriptive values include overall 50-patient scores: SUM worst 27.2 (SD 9.0), study 17.3 (SD 10.3); GHQ worst 14.7 (SD 6.9), study 8.6 (SD 4.3); PQ worst 12.4 (SD 3.4), study 8.6 (SD 4.3). Table 1 and Table 2 contain ANOVA mean squares, including PQ, GHQ, and SUM terms, but no direct treatment effect estimates or confidence intervals. The 6-month completion counts were 19 total, with 10 in one sequence and 9 in the other.

record.summary: This two-arm randomized trial compared online CBT delivered by FITNET-NHS with remotely delivered Activity Management in adolescents aged 11–17 years with ME/CFS. FITNET-NHS improved physical function more at 6 months, with an adjusted mean difference of 8.2 points (95% CI 2.7 to 13.6), and increased school attendance by approximately half a day per week. It also produced slightly more QALYs but substantially higher costs and was unlikely to be cost-effective at £20,000 per QALY.

record.summary: In 314 adolescents with ME/CFS, remotely delivered FITNET-NHS cognitive-behavioural therapy was compared with videocall Activity Management. At 6 months, physical function was significantly better with FITNET-NHS by 8.2 points (95% CI 2.7 to 13.6; p=0.003), but the difference was not clearly sustained at 12 months. FITNET-NHS also improved school attendance but was more costly and unlikely to be cost-effective.

record.summary: This two-arm randomized trial compared online CBT delivered by FITNET-NHS with remotely delivered Activity Management in adolescents aged 11–17 years with ME/CFS. FITNET-NHS improved physical function more at 6 months, with an adjusted mean difference of 8.2 points (95% CI 2.7 to 13.6), and increased school attendance by approximately half a day per week. It also produced slightly more QALYs but substantially higher costs and was unlikely to be cost-effective at £20,000 per QALY.

Adverse-event cases were not assigned to study arms.

record.summary: In adults with CDC-defined CFS, 60 days of low- or high-dose cistanche/ginkgo supplementation produced significant overall between-group effects for blood ammonia and lactic acid, but not for glucose, free fatty acids, creatine kinase, C-reactive protein, estradiol, or testosterone. Changes in blood glucose and lactic acid were significantly associated with product effectiveness, while liver and kidney safety biomarkers remained within normal ranges without significant group differences.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Extracted Tables 6–8 and the adjacent results paragraph only. Table 6 reports mean ± SD except estradiol, for which medians are reported because data were highly skewed. Table 7 reports logistic-regression associations rather than arm-level contrasts. Table 8 reports safety biomarkers for 175 completers but does not provide per-arm sample sizes. Source filename: 10.3389--fnut.2021.658630.xml.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Among 53 participants with NRS ≥63, change was 39.5 ± 21.0 with Myelophil versus 25.7 ± 19.6 with placebo; p = 0.017.
In the severe subgroup, physical NRS change was 25.3 ± 12.6 versus 16.5 ± 12.8; p = 0.016.
In the severe subgroup, mental NRS change was 14.3 ± 9.1 versus 8.9 ± 7.4; p = 0.021.
Severe-subgroup VAS change was 4.2 ± 2.5 versus 2.8 ± 2.5; p = 0.069.
Severe-subgroup FSS change was 21.7 ± 14.2 versus 10.7 ± 11.9; p = 0.004.
Severe-subgroup SF-36 increased by 19.9 ± 18.5 versus 10.4 ± 15.6; p = 0.050.
No significant difference was observed between Myelophil and placebo groups; data not shown.

record.summary: This double-blind randomized trial tested 12 weeks of oral Myelophil in adults with CDC-defined CFS against matching placebo. The prespecified total-population analysis did not show statistically significant benefit, but a post hoc subgroup with more severe fatigue showed significant improvement across several fatigue-related outcomes. Myelophil was generally well tolerated; three of 48 participants reported mild diarrhea.

The section reports 98 total participants, 38 males and 60 females, and a 53-participant post hoc severe-fatigue subgroup.

record.summary: In adults with fibromyalgia, with or without chronic fatigue syndrome, the Synchronize+ multicomponent intervention was compared with usual care. At 3 months, the intervention group showed statistically significant improvements in moderate-to-vigorous and total physical activity, lower-body strength, 6-minute walk distance, sleep, and perceived exertion, while changes in sedentary behaviour and hand-grip strength were not statistically significant.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 reports baseline, 3-month follow-up, change values, confidence intervals, and p-values separately for each arm; the p-values appear to be within-arm values. Follow-up sample sizes per arm were not reported. The sedentary behaviour outcome was from a subsample (n = 67). Some table confidence intervals appear internally inconsistent or reversed and were preserved as printed.

record.summary: This pragmatic randomized trial tested a 2-week Synchronize+ multicomponent rehabilitation intervention against usual care in adults with fibromyalgia, including participants with chronic fatigue syndrome. At 3 months, the intervention significantly improved physical activity, sleep, lower-body strength, 6MWT distance, and perceived exertion, while sedentary behaviour and handgrip strength were not statistically significant.

record.summary: In adults with mild to moderate CFS, individual standard CBT and shorter interpersonal CBT improved participant-rated overall health compared with waiting-list control after intervention. Positive change was reported by 33% with standard CBT, 26% with interpersonal CBT, and 8% with waiting-list control; odds ratios versus control were 5.5 and 4.1, respectively, with statistically significant p-values. Benefits were sustained at 1 year, although the waiting-list group was not assessed then.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Source section contains Table 5 and discussion only. Table 5 provides categorical CGI data and odds ratios, not means or SDs. Per-arm totals were calculated by summing category counts. WLC was not assessed at 1-year follow-up. Discussion reports overall percentages of participants with SF-36 physical function score >=75 and fatigue in the normal range, but no per-arm values.

per_arm.flow_source_quote: Twelve subjects did not attend the baseline visit: nine (five in the experimental group and four in the placebo group) of their own accord and three (all from the experimental group) were considered lost due to limited mobility (spinal surgery, ankle sprain and low back pain, respectively). A total of 60 participants (placebo,  n  = 32 and experimental group,  n  = 28) were visited at baseline, but only 50 (83%) completed the final assessment at 20 weeks; three participants (5%) were lost to follow-up (one in the placebo group with flares of the disease, one in the experimental group with erythematous rash from taking ibuprofen and another scheduled for hip surgery) and seven (12%) abandoned the study at their own request (five in the placebo group and two in the experimental group). The remaining ME/CFS patients completed all the study protocol procedures and were included in the analyses of outcome measures ( Figure 1 ).

risk_of_bias.key_concern: The report analyzed only completers (50 of 72 randomized), with substantial pre-baseline and follow-up attrition and no available prespecified analysis plan.

summary: This double-blind pilot RCT randomized 72 female adults with Fukuda-defined ME/CFS to 16 weeks of oral melatonin 1 mg plus zinc 10 mg daily or matching placebo; 50 completed follow-up. The melatonin-zinc group had a significantly better FIS-40 physical-domain result versus placebo at 16 weeks (p=0.026), but the paper reported no numerical FIS-40 values. Most SF-36, PSQI, and HADS between-group comparisons were not significant; urinary aMT6s was markedly higher with melatonin-zinc during treatment (both p<0.0001).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: FIS-40 quantitative values were presented only in Figure 3 and are not numerically extractable from supplied text; reported FIS p-values were retained. Tables 2-5 report mean ± SEM, not SD. Table 1 BMI dispersion is reported as ±SD per footnote despite implausibly small values. Some later outcome objects use shared timepoint IDs 1=baseline, 2=8 weeks, 3=16 weeks, 4=4 weeks post-treatment.
